q:
Mara checked the supply cart twice before her shift began, then a third time after report. When the charge nurse asked why, Mara pointed to a note taped inside the top drawer. The reminder, written in her own handwriting, dated from the night a missing suction catheter had cost the team four minutes during an emergency. "I'd rather lose thirty seconds now," she said. The charge nurse nodded slowly. The following week, a cart check appeared on the start-of-shift list for every nurse on the unit.

Which conclusion about Mara is best supported by the passage?
o: She does not trust the other nurses on the unit to stock the supply cart correctly.
She was the nurse responsible for the missing catheter on the night of the emergency.
She was asked by the charge nurse to train the other nurses to check their carts.
A past delay she witnessed shapes the way she prepares for each of her shifts.
w: The note recalls the night a missing catheter cost four minutes, and Mara says she would rather lose thirty seconds now. Her repeated checks are explained by that earlier delay.

n.0: Nothing in the passage blames other nurses; her checks are tied to one past event, not to distrust of coworkers.
n.1: The note is in her handwriting, but the passage never says who left the catheter out; this is an assumption.
n.2: The charge nurse added a cart check to the shift list; the passage never says Mara was asked to train anyone.

q:
Westbrook Clinic offered walk-in flu shots this fall for the first time, in addition to scheduled appointments. The table shows the percentage of the clinic's patients in each age group who received a flu shot at the clinic.
Age group | Last year | This year
18 to 34 | 22% | 35%
35 to 64 | 41% | 47%
65 and older | 68% | 69%
The clinic manager plans to keep walk-in hours next year.

Which conclusions are supported by the passage and table? Select all that apply.
o: More patients aged 35 to 64 got a shot this year than patients aged 65 and older.
The youngest age group showed the largest increase in its vaccination rate.
Walk-in hours caused the rise in vaccination among patients aged 18 to 34.
Older patients used the walk-in hours more often than younger patients did.
Patients 65 and older had the highest vaccination rate of the three groups this year.
The percentage of patients who got a flu shot rose in each age group this year.
w: Every group rose (22 to 35, 41 to 47, 68 to 69). The 18 to 34 group gained 13 points, more than 6 or 1. At 69%, patients 65 and older had the highest rate this year.

n.0: The table gives percentages, not numbers of patients; without group sizes the counts cannot be compared.
n.2: Walk-in hours began the same year, but the table shows only rates, not why they changed; causation is not established.
n.3: The table does not separate walk-in shots from scheduled ones, so use of walk-in hours by age is unknown.

q:
A school district surveyed 1,200 high school students about sleep. Students who used their phones in bed after 10 p.m. reported sleeping about 50 minutes less on school nights than students who did not, even though both groups reported going to bed at similar times. The district then launched a campaign urging families to charge phones outside the bedroom. Early results from 80 families who joined a trial of the campaign show that the students fell asleep about 20 minutes sooner on average.

Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
o: Students who use phones in bed go to bed later than students who do not use them.
Students who join the campaign can expect to gain about 50 minutes of sleep on school nights.
Phone use in bed may delay sleep even when students go to bed at the same time as their peers.
Most high school students in the district probably use their phones in bed after 10 p.m.
w: Both groups went to bed at similar times, yet phone users slept about 50 minutes less, and removing phones helped trial students fall asleep sooner. Together these details support the idea that phone use delays falling asleep.

n.0: This contradicts the passage, which says both groups reported going to bed at similar times.
n.1: This over-extends the data: 50 minutes was the survey gap, but the trial showed students falling asleep about 20 minutes sooner.
n.3: The passage gives no share of students who use phones in bed, so a majority cannot be concluded.

q:
To cut absences from stomach illness, Lincoln Elementary placed handwashing posters above every sink in October. The school nurse also taught a five-minute handwashing lesson in each classroom. From October through March, absences linked to stomach illness fell by 30 percent compared with the same months the year before. Absences at two nearby schools that made no changes stayed about the same. The custodians also reported that the soap dispensers needed refilling nearly twice as often as in past years.

The principal concludes that students washed their hands more often after the changes. Which detail best supports this conclusion?
o: The school nurse taught a five-minute handwashing lesson in each classroom.
Absences at two nearby schools that made no changes stayed about the same.
Absences linked to stomach illness fell by 30 percent from October through March.
Soap dispensers needed refilling nearly twice as often as in past years.
w: The conclusion is about a behavior: washing hands more often. Soap use nearly doubling is a direct measure of that behavior, so it gives the strongest support.

n.0: The lesson describes what the school did, not what students then did.
n.1: The comparison schools help rule out a seasonal explanation for fewer absences, but they say nothing about handwashing at Lincoln.
n.2: Fewer absences is an outcome that could have other causes; it supports the claim that illness fell, not that washing increased.

q:
Greenway Pharmacy opened a drive-through window in June. The manager tracked the average wait from a customer's arrival to pickup.
Month | Counter wait | Drive-through wait
May | 14 min | not open
June | 11 min | 6 min
July | 10 min | 9 min
August | 10 min | 12 min
The manager noted that drive-through use grew each month as word spread, while one employee continued to staff the window.

Which conclusion is best supported by the passage and table?
o: As use of the drive-through grew, its wait became longer than the wait at the counter.
Opening the drive-through cut the counter wait by 4 minutes in each month after May.
Customers prefer the counter to the drive-through because the counter wait is shorter.
Adding a second employee at the window would bring the drive-through wait back to 6 minutes.
w: Drive-through use grew every month with one employee, and its wait rose from 6 to 9 to 12 minutes. By August it was longer than the 10-minute counter wait.

n.1: The counter wait fell by 3 minutes in June (14 to 11) and by 4 in July and August, so it did not drop by 4 in each month.
n.2: The passage says drive-through use grew each month, which does not suggest customers prefer the counter.
n.3: This is a prediction the data cannot test; staffing never changed, so the effect of a second employee is unknown.

q:
Subject: Fire inspection moved to Tuesday
Hi everyone. The fire marshal's visit has moved up from Thursday to Tuesday at 9 a.m. Please have all hallways clear of linen carts and wheelchairs by the end of the Monday evening shift. At our last inspection, we were cited for two blocked exits on the third floor, and the marshal warned that a second citation would bring a fine. I will walk the third floor myself on Monday at 6 p.m. to check the exits. Thank you for your help.
Dana Ruiz, Facilities

Which conclusion is best supported by the email?
o: Dana is especially concerned about the condition of the third floor before Tuesday.
The inspection was moved up because Facilities asked the marshal for an earlier date.
Linen carts may be returned to the hallways once the marshal has left the building.
The fire marshal fined the facility for the two blocked exits on the third floor.
w: Dana mentions the earlier third-floor citation, the risk of a fine, and her plan to walk that floor personally on Monday. Together these show special concern about the third floor.

n.1: The email does not say why the date changed; the reason is not given.
n.2: The email says nothing about what happens after the inspection; this is an unsupported assumption.
n.3: The email says a second citation would bring a fine, which means the first citation did not.

q:
Vitamin D is unusual among vitamins because the body can make it. When skin is exposed to the ultraviolet B (UVB) rays in sunlight, it produces a form of vitamin D that the liver and kidneys then activate. The amount of UVB reaching the ground depends on the angle of the sun. In winter, at places north of about 37 degrees latitude, the sun sits so low that little UVB reaches the ground, and the skin makes little vitamin D however long a person stays outside. Foods such as fatty fish, eggs, and fortified milk also supply the vitamin. Harborview lies at 42 degrees north latitude; Palmetto lies at 33 degrees north.

Based on the passage, which conclusion is best supported?
o: Residents of Harborview can make up for winter by spending more hours outdoors.
Winter sunlight gives Harborview residents less vitamin D than it gives Palmetto residents.
Residents of Harborview have lower vitamin D levels all year than residents of Palmetto.
Residents of Palmetto do not need vitamin D from food during the winter months.
w: Two details combine: north of about 37 degrees, winter sun produces little vitamin D in skin, and Harborview (42 degrees) is north of that line while Palmetto (33 degrees) is south of it.

n.0: This contradicts the passage: north of 37 degrees in winter, the skin makes little vitamin D however long a person stays outside.
n.2: The passage limits the latitude effect to winter and says food also supplies vitamin D, so year-round levels cannot be concluded.
n.3: The passage says Palmetto residents can make vitamin D from winter sun, but it does not say they need none from food.

q:
Two years ago, Cedar Ridge Hospital began letting its nurses choose either 8-hour or 12-hour shifts. In a recent staff survey, 70 percent of nurses on 12-hour shifts said they had more days available for family, compared with 35 percent of nurses on 8-hour shifts. However, 40 percent of nurses on 12-hour shifts said they felt very tired at the end of a shift, compared with 25 percent of those on 8-hour shifts. The rate at which nurses left the hospital was similar in both groups.

Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
o: Most nurses at Cedar Ridge Hospital now prefer 12-hour shifts to 8-hour shifts.
Nurses on 8-hour shifts are less likely than others to leave the hospital.
Nurses on 12-hour shifts tend to trade more fatigue for more days with family.
Twelve-hour shifts lead to more patient care errors than 8-hour shifts.
w: Nurses on 12-hour shifts were twice as likely to report more family days (70% vs 35%) and also more likely to feel very tired (40% vs 25%), so the passage supports a trade-off.

n.0: The passage gives survey results within each group but not how many nurses chose each shift, so preference cannot be concluded.
n.1: This contradicts the passage, which says the rate of leaving was similar in both groups.
n.3: Patient errors are never mentioned; this relies on outside assumptions rather than the text.

q:
Rosa had worked weekend shifts at the hardware store since March, and every paycheck went into an envelope marked CAR. She had already turned down a beach trip in June and skipped the new phone that her friends all bought. By August, the envelope held $2,600 of the $3,000 her uncle was asking for his old sedan. On Friday, her friend Tasha called with news: she had two spare tickets to a concert in the city on Saturday, $150 each, and she wanted Rosa to come.

Based on the passage, how will Rosa most likely respond to Tasha's offer?
o: She will ask Tasha to lend her the money until her next paycheck arrives.
She will turn down the ticket so that she can keep saving for the car.
She will buy the ticket and ask her uncle to lower his price for the sedan.
She will accept the ticket because she has nearly reached her savings goal.
w: Rosa has repeatedly given up treats (a beach trip, a new phone) to save for the car and is still $400 short. Her established pattern points to declining the $150 ticket.

n.0: Borrowing from Tasha has no basis in the text and runs against her habit of saving every paycheck.
n.2: This needs an event the passage never suggests: nothing indicates the uncle would change his price.
n.3: Being close to the goal does not reverse her pattern; she is still $400 short, and nothing suggests she would stop saving now.

q:
The town of Brookfield added a Route 9 bus to its east side three years ago. The table shows average riders per weekday.
Year | Route 9 riders | All routes combined
Year 1 | 420 | 5,100
Year 2 | 610 | 5,350
Year 3 | 800 | 5,560
A town report says Route 9's growth came mostly from new apartment buildings along its path. Two more buildings on the route are scheduled to open next year, and no other changes to bus service are planned.

Which prediction is best supported by the passage and table?
o: Route 9 ridership will most likely keep rising next year as the new buildings open.
Route 9 will carry more riders next year than all of the other routes put together.
Ridership on all routes combined will climb to about 8,000 riders per weekday next year.
Riders from other routes will likely switch to Route 9, lowering ridership on those routes.
w: Route 9 grew by about 190 riders a year, the report ties that growth to new apartment buildings on the route, and two more buildings open next year. The cause is still in motion, so continued growth is the supported prediction.

n.1: The other routes carry about 4,760 riders; Route 9 would need to grow sixfold in one year to pass them.
n.2: Combined ridership grew by about 200 to 250 a year; a jump of about 2,400 over-extends the trend.
n.3: Ridership on the other routes rose slightly each year (4,680, 4,740, 4,760), so the trend does not show riders leaving them.

q:
Basic Sandwich Bread
1. Dissolve the yeast in water heated to between 105 and 115 °F. Water hotter than 130 °F kills yeast. Water cooler than 70 °F slows the yeast, so the dough rises much more slowly.
2. Stir in the flour, salt, and oil, and knead for 8 minutes.
3. Cover the bowl and let the dough rise until it has doubled in size, about 1 hour in a warm kitchen.
4. Shape the loaf and bake at 375 °F for 30 minutes.
Jamal follows every step but dissolves the yeast in tap water that is 60 °F.

Based on the recipe, what will most likely happen?
o: His dough will take longer than about an hour to double in size.
His dough will rise faster because cool water protects the yeast.
His dough will fail to rise because the cool water will kill the yeast.
His loaf will need less than 30 minutes of baking time to finish.
w: Step 1 says water cooler than 70 °F slows the yeast so the dough rises much more slowly. At 60 °F, Jamal's dough should take longer than the usual hour to double.

n.1: This reverses the recipe, which says cool water makes the dough rise more slowly.
n.2: The recipe says water hotter than 130 °F kills yeast; cool water slows it instead.
n.3: Nothing in the recipe links water temperature to baking time; this prediction has no support.

q:
The Marlow River Bridge will close for repairs on June 1 and stay closed for three months. During the closure, drivers will detour across the Oak Street Bridge, two miles north. When the Marlow bridge closed for one weekend last fall, a traffic study found that travel times across the Oak Street Bridge doubled during morning and evening rush hours, while midday traffic was barely affected. The city has asked large employers to consider flexible start times during the repairs.

Which prediction about the summer is best supported by the passage?
o: Midday trips across the Oak Street Bridge will likely take about double their usual time.
Rush-hour trips across the Oak Street Bridge will likely take longer than usual.
The repairs will last longer than three months because of the heavy detour traffic.
Large employers will require their workers to start later until the bridge reopens.
w: The weekend study showed Oak Street travel times doubling at rush hour when the Marlow bridge closed. A three-month closure puts the same cause in motion, so longer rush-hour trips are the supported prediction.

n.0: This uses the wrong part of the study: travel times doubled at rush hour, while midday traffic was barely affected.
n.2: The passage gives no reason to expect the repairs to run over; traffic on the detour does not affect the repair schedule.
n.3: The city only asked employers to consider flexible start times; a requirement is not supported.

q:
Every evening, Mr. Okafor walked the length of his garden and studied the sky over the western ridge. The farmers in the valley joked that he trusted clouds more than the radio. That afternoon, the radio had promised a dry night. But as he finished his walk, he watched the swallows skim low over the field and felt the first cool gust that, in his experience, came about an hour before a storm. He stood still for a long moment, then turned toward the shed where he kept the canvas covers.

What will Mr. Okafor most likely do next?
o: Leave his plants uncovered because the radio predicted a dry night.
Ask the valley farmers whether they also expect a storm tonight.
Cover his plants because he expects a storm despite the forecast.
Harvest his ripest vegetables before a hard frost arrives tonight.
w: The passage says he trusts the sky over the radio, he notices the gust that usually comes before a storm, and he heads for the shed with the canvas covers. All point to covering his plants.

n.0: He turns toward the canvas covers, and he is known to trust the sky over the radio, so he is unlikely to rely on the forecast.
n.1: Nothing suggests he will consult anyone; he trusts his own reading of the sky and is already heading to the shed.
n.3: The signs he notices point to a storm; the passage mentions no cold or frost.

q:
Starting next month, Summit Medical Group will ask patients to complete their check-in forms online before they arrive. Patients who arrive without completing the form can fill it out on a tablet in the waiting room, which takes about 10 minutes. During a three-month pilot at one office, average check-in time at the front desk fell from 7 minutes to 2 minutes for patients who completed the form at home. About a third of the patients in the pilot arrived without completing it.

Which prediction is best supported by the passage?
o: Summit will remove the waiting-room tablets after next month because few patients use them.
Many patients will stop booking appointments with Summit because of the new form.
Patients who skip the online form will likely take longer to check in than those who complete it.
Average check-in time at each Summit office will likely fall to about 2 minutes per patient.
w: Patients who completed the form at home checked in in about 2 minutes, while those who arrive without it need about 10 minutes on a tablet. The passage supports a longer check-in for patients who skip the form.

n.0: About a third of pilot patients needed the tablet, so the passage suggests the tablets will be used, not removed.
n.1: Nothing in the passage suggests patients will leave; this prediction has no support.
n.3: Two minutes applied to patients who completed the form; with about a third arriving without it, the overall average would be higher.

q:
The Pine Lake reservoir supplies water to the town of Alder. The town's drought plan has three stages: Stage 1 (voluntary water conservation) begins when the reservoir falls below 70 percent of capacity, Stage 2 (lawn watering limited to two days a week) below 60 percent, and Stage 3 (no lawn watering) below 50 percent.
Date | Reservoir level
June 1 | 74%
July 1 | 68%
August 1 | 62%
Forecasters expect August to be as dry as July, and water use in town has stayed steady all summer.

If the pattern continues, which stage will most likely be in effect on September 1?
o: Stage 3, with lawn watering banned
Stage 2, with lawn watering two days a week
No stage, as rain refills the reservoir
Stage 1, with voluntary water conservation
w: Step 1: the level fell 6 points each month (74 to 68 to 62), and conditions are unchanged, so September 1 should be about 56 percent. Step 2: 56 percent is below 60 but above 50, which is Stage 2.

n.0: Stage 3 needs a level below 50 percent; at 6 points a month the reservoir should reach about 56 percent.
n.2: Forecasters expect another dry month and water use is steady, so nothing supports a reversal of the trend.
n.3: Stage 1 is the stage in effect on August 1 (62 percent); after another month of decline the level should drop below 60.

q:
Last year, the Oakmont Public Library stopped charging late fines on children's books. Over the next twelve months, the share of children's books returned within two weeks of the due date rose from 81 percent to 88 percent, and the number of new children's library cards rose by 12 percent. The library still charged fines on adult books, and that fine revenue stayed about the same. This month, the library board voted to end late fines on adult books as well, starting in January.

Which predictions are supported by the passage? Select all that apply.
o: Fine revenue from adult books will most likely drop after January.
Children's books will soon fall back to an 81 percent return rate.
Timely returns of adult books may improve after January, as they did for children's books.
The library will probably cut staff hours next year to make up for the lost fine revenue.
Adult books will most likely be returned late more often once their fines end.
w: Ending fines on children's books was followed by better returns, so a similar change for adult books may have a similar result. And once adult fines end, the adult fine revenue the library has been collecting will fall.

n.1: Nothing suggests the children's policy will change, so a reversal of the trend has no stated cause.
n.3: Staff cuts require an unstated event; the passage never mentions budgets or staffing.
n.4: The only evidence, from children's books, shows timely returns rising after fines ended; nothing points to more late returns.

q:
How to use your inhaler
This medicine works best when it reaches deep into your lungs. Breathe out fully, seal your lips around the mouthpiece, and press the canister as you begin a slow, deep breath. Then hold your breath for 10 seconds. If you breathe in quickly, much of the medicine lands on the back of your throat instead of reaching your lungs, and over time you may notice a hoarse voice. Rinse your mouth with water after each use to remove any medicine left in your mouth.

Devon presses the canister and then takes a quick, sharp breath each time he uses his inhaler. Based on the leaflet, what is most likely to happen?
o: Less of the medicine will reach his lungs, and his voice may become hoarse.
The medicine will reach his lungs faster and so begin to work sooner.
He will need to hold his breath longer than 10 seconds to make up for it.
Rinsing his mouth will carry the medicine from his throat to his lungs.
w: The leaflet says a quick breath leaves much of the medicine on the back of the throat instead of in the lungs and may cause a hoarse voice over time.

n.1: This reverses the leaflet: a quick breath sends less medicine to the lungs, not more.
n.2: The leaflet offers no longer breath-hold as a fix; the fix it implies is a slow, deep breath.
n.3: The leaflet says rinsing removes medicine left in the mouth; it does not move medicine to the lungs.

q:
For five years, Northline Grocery has followed the same pattern. Each spring it opens a new store in a town where its home delivery service has already grown past 500 customers. This year, delivery customers passed 500 in two towns, Carver and Danbury. Northline has signed a lease on an empty building in Carver that once housed a furniture store. A local news report says Danbury has no available building large enough for a grocery store, and no new construction is planned there.

Which prediction is best supported by the passage?
o: Northline will most likely open new stores in both Carver and Danbury next spring.
Northline will end its delivery service in Carver once the store opens.
Northline will most likely open a new store in Carver next spring.
Northline will open a store in Danbury before it opens one in Carver.
w: Carver meets Northline's usual condition (over 500 delivery customers) and the company has already leased a building there, so a spring opening in Carver fits the five-year pattern.

n.0: Danbury meets the customer condition, but it has no suitable building and no planned construction, so a store there next spring is not supported.
n.1: The passage says nothing about ending delivery after a store opens; this needs an unstated event.
n.3: Danbury lacks a building while Carver has a signed lease, so the passage points the other way.

q:
In a 12-week study, 60 adults who walked briskly for 30 minutes a day lowered their average resting heart rate from 76 to 70 beats per minute. A comparison group of 60 adults who kept their usual routines showed no change. After the study ended, researchers checked on the walkers for another 12 weeks. Walkers who stopped their daily walks returned to about their starting heart rates by the end of that period, while those who kept walking stayed near 70.

Lena was one of the walkers, and she plans to stop walking when the study ends. Based on the passage, what will most likely happen to her resting heart rate over the next 12 weeks?
o: It will probably stay near 70 because she completed the full 12 weeks of walking.
It will keep falling below 70 because the benefits of walking build over time.
It will rise above 76 because stopping exercise suddenly strains the heart.
It will probably drift back toward the rate she had before the study.
w: The follow-up found that walkers who stopped returned to about their starting heart rates within 12 weeks. Lena fits that group, so her rate should drift back toward where it began.

n.0: Staying near 70 applied to walkers who kept walking, not to those who stopped.
n.1: The passage shows no further drop after walking stops; this reverses the follow-up finding.
n.2: Walkers who stopped returned to about their starting rates; nothing suggests they rose above them.

q:
Puzzle Port, a smartphone game, launched in March. The table shows weekly downloads.
Week | Event | Downloads
March 1 | Launch | 9,000
March 15 | none | 4,100
April 12 | Update with new levels | 8,600
April 26 | none | 4,300
May 24 | Update with new levels | 8,900
June 7 | none | 4,200
The company has announced its next update with new levels for the week of July 5, with no other changes planned.

Which prediction is best supported by the passage and table?
o: Downloads will drop after July 5 because players dislike frequent updates.
Downloads will peak in the weeks before July 5 as players hear about the update.
Downloads will spike in the week of July 5 and fall back within about two weeks.
Downloads will rise each week through the rest of the summer after July 5.
w: Each launch or update produced a jump to roughly 8,600 to 9,000 downloads that fell back to about 4,000 within two weeks. The next update should follow the same pattern.

n.0: Downloads rose after every earlier update; nothing in the table suggests players dislike updates.
n.1: In the table, downloads rose in the update weeks themselves, not before them.
n.3: Earlier spikes faded within two weeks rather than building, so steady growth reverses the established pattern.

q:
For three years, Priya and Elena had finished first and second at the county science fair, always in that order. This spring, Priya's solar oven cracked the night before judging. At ten o'clock, Elena knocked on her door with a roll of foil, a glue gun, and her own notes on insulation. They worked until midnight. The next day Elena took first place, and Priya took third. Walking out of the gym, Priya expected to feel crushed. Instead, she found herself planning next year's project with Elena, and the ribbon in her pocket felt lighter than she had expected.

Which statement best expresses the theme of the passage?
o: Kindness from a rival can turn a competition into a friendship.
The long rivalry between two students at a county science fair
Elena helps Priya repair her solar oven on the night before the science fair.
Hard work is the surest path to winning first place in a contest.
w: A theme is a message about life stated as a complete idea. Elena's help changes Priya's feelings about losing and leads to shared plans, so the story's message is that a rival's kindness can build friendship.

n.1: This names the topic of the story in a phrase; it does not state a message about it.
n.2: This is a plot summary of one event, not the message the story conveys.
n.3: Priya worked hard yet placed third; the story's focus is the friendship, not a recipe for winning.

q:
The Lot on Fifth Street
They paved the field where I used to run,
poured gray over clover, wall over sun.
But one old oak they could not move
still splits the sidewalk, groove by groove.
Each spring it pushes, slow and sure,
a crack, a root, a little more,
till weeds and sparrows find the seam
and green comes back like a half-remembered dream.

Which theme does the poem express?
o: Nature can slowly reclaim what people have tried to cover over.
Childhood memories fade as familiar places change over time.
The speaker regrets having moved away from the old field.
Cities should protect their oldest trees from new construction.
w: The poem moves from paving over the field to the oak slowly splitting the sidewalk until weeds and birds return. Its message is nature's slow return through what people built.

n.1: The poem's central movement is the oak and weeds breaking back through the pavement; its one image of memory describes the green returning, not the speaker's memories fading.
n.2: The poem never says the speaker moved away; regret about leaving is not in the text.
n.3: This is a policy recommendation; the poem describes and reflects but never argues for protecting trees.

q:
Passage 1
At mile 22 of her first marathon, Gloria's left calf cramped so badly that she sat down on the curb. Volunteers offered her a ride to the finish. She shook her head, stood, and walked, then jogged, one streetlight at a time. She crossed the line after the clocks had been switched off.

Passage 2
When the river flooded the Ashton library, it ruined 30,000 books. For eight months, volunteers sorted donations on folding tables in the high school gym, a few boxes each evening. Last week, the library reopened with full shelves and a new reading room.

Which theme do both passages share?
o: Finishing a hard race matters more than the time on the clock.
Steady effort, step by step, can carry people through great difficulty.
Floods and other disasters test the resources of small towns.
Communities grow stronger when neighbors give their time to one another.
w: Gloria finishes by going one streetlight at a time, and the library is rebuilt a few boxes each evening over eight months. Both show persistence in small steps overcoming a setback.

n.0: This fits Passage 1 only; Passage 2 is not about a race.
n.2: This names a topic of Passage 2 and does not apply to Passage 1.
n.3: Community volunteering fits Passage 2, but Gloria turns down help and finishes on her own.

q:
Passage 1
When I was ten, summer meant leaving the house after breakfast and coming home when the streetlights blinked on. We built forts in the creek bed and settled our arguments ourselves. Those long, unsupervised afternoons taught me how to be a friend.

Passage 2
Every Tuesday night, 12-year-old Amir logs on to a coding club with kids from four states. They debug each other's games, tease each other in the chat, and celebrate birthdays on video. Two of them met in person for the first time this summer and hugged like old friends.

How do the themes of the two passages differ?
o: Passage 1 is about friendship, while Passage 2 is about learning to write code.
Both passages suggest that children today are lonelier than children once were.
Passage 1 rejects technology, while Passage 2 rejects outdoor play for children.
Passage 1 ties friendship to outdoor play; Passage 2 shows it growing through screens.
w: Both passages are about how children form friendships. Passage 1 credits unsupervised outdoor play; Passage 2 shows close friendships forming in an online coding club.

n.0: Coding is the setting of Passage 2, but its central idea is friendship, the same subject as Passage 1.
n.1: Passage 2 shows children who are close and connected, so loneliness is not a shared theme.
n.2: This overstates both: Passage 1 never criticizes technology, and Passage 2 never criticizes outdoor play.

q:
Passage 1
A young beaver tried to build a dam alone. Each night the current carried away his branches, and each morning he began again, too proud to call the older beavers downstream. At last, worn out, he asked. By sunset, five of them had built what he had failed to build in a week.

Passage 2
In her first month as a new graduate nurse, Kim stayed late every night to finish her charting. She was sure that asking her preceptor for shortcuts would look weak. When she finally asked, her preceptor showed her how to chart at the bedside, and Kim began leaving on time. "I wish I had asked in week one," she said.

Which theme is developed in both passages?
o: Pride can keep people from help that would make their work easier.
Experienced workers should seek out newcomers who need training.
Working longer hours is the surest way to master a new task.
Animals and people learn new skills in very different ways.
w: The beaver is too proud to ask the older beavers, and Kim fears that asking will look weak. In both, asking finally solves the problem, so both develop the idea that pride blocks useful help.

n.1: Neither text says experienced workers should seek out newcomers; in both, the newcomer finally asks.
n.2: Both texts show long hours failing; success comes from asking for help.
n.3: The passages show the beaver and Kim learning the same lesson, so they are parallel, not contrasted.

q:
Passage 1
From the school nurse: Students who eat breakfast tend to pay closer attention during morning classes. But not every breakfast helps equally. A meal with protein and whole grains, such as eggs and toast, keeps energy steady until lunch, while a frosted pastry often leads to a slump by mid-morning.

Passage 2
From a nutrition column: Studies on breakfast and body weight have produced mixed results, and skipping breakfast does not appear to cause weight gain by itself. What people eat over the whole day matters more. A sugary muffin at 7 a.m. is no better a choice than waiting until a balanced lunch.

Which idea is expressed in both passages?
o: The kind of food eaten matters, not simply whether a meal is eaten.
Eating breakfast improves students' attention during morning classes.
Skipping breakfast has little effect on a person's body weight.
Breakfast is the most important meal of the day for good health.
w: Passage 1 contrasts eggs and toast with a frosted pastry; Passage 2 says a sugary muffin is no better than waiting for a balanced lunch. Both stress food quality over the fact of eating.

n.1: This is the central claim of Passage 1 only; Passage 2 does not discuss attention.
n.2: This comes from Passage 2 only; Passage 1 does not discuss weight.
n.3: Neither passage says this; Passage 2 suggests breakfast is not essential for weight.

q:
Passage 1
Every Sunday, Abuela Rosa rolled tamales with her granddaughter Lucia, naming each step in Spanish. After Abuela died, Lucia found that she could still hear the words as her hands moved through the folding. Now she teaches the steps, in Spanish, to her own son.

Passage 2
My father kept his grandfather's fishing net long after the family boat was sold. When I asked why, he showed me how to mend it, knot by knot, the way his grandfather had shown him. I have never fished for a living, but I still mend nets each winter, and with each knot I picture my great-grandfather's hands at work.

Which themes are shared by both passages? Select all that apply.
o: Practical skills matter more than the money they can earn.
Language is the most important part of a family's heritage.
Repeating a family task can keep a loved one present in memory.
Children tend to reject the traditions their parents value.
Traditions passed down by hand keep a link to earlier generations.
Grief over a loss is eased by joining a new community.
w: In both, a hands-on skill (folding tamales, mending nets) is taught across generations, and doing it brings an ancestor to mind: Lucia hears Abuela's words, and the narrator pictures his great-grandfather's hands.

n.0: Passage 2 mentions not fishing for a living, but neither passage compares skills with money.
n.1: Language appears only in Passage 1, and neither passage ranks it as the most important part of heritage.
n.3: Both passages show children keeping traditions, the opposite of rejecting them.
n.5: Neither passage involves joining a new community; Lucia's comfort comes from a family practice.

q:
Marcus signed up to volunteer at Maple Court Senior Living because his school required twenty service hours. For the first few Thursdays, he read the newspaper aloud to Mr. Hale, who corrected his pronunciation and rarely smiled. Marcus counted the minutes. In October, Mr. Hale mentioned that he had once flown cargo planes in Alaska. Curious, Marcus asked a question, and then another. By December, Marcus had logged sixty hours, far more than he needed, and had filled a notebook with Mr. Hale's stories.

Which statement expresses a theme of the passage rather than its topic or plot?
o: A high school student's volunteer work at a senior living center
Marcus logs sixty hours after he begins asking Mr. Hale about Alaska.
Schools should require students to complete community service hours.
Curiosity about others can turn an obligation into a real connection.
w: A theme is a general message stated as a full sentence. Marcus's attitude changes when he becomes curious about Mr. Hale, turning required hours into a relationship he values.

n.0: This phrase names the topic; it states no message.
n.1: This retells events from the plot rather than stating a general message.
n.2: This is an opinion about school policy; the story never argues for requiring service hours.

q:
Passage 1
When Nadia's best friend Jo copied her homework, Nadia told the teacher she had shared her answers by accident. The teacher believed her. Jo kept copying, and by spring both girls were called in for a meeting with the principal. Afterward, Jo admitted she wished Nadia had just told her no.

Passage 2
Theo asked Sam what he thought of the song he had written. "Honestly? The chorus is boring," Sam said, and laughed. Theo did not touch his guitar for a week. Later, Sam tried again. He told Theo which lines he loved and suggested a faster beat for the chorus. Theo rewrote it that night.

How do the themes of the two passages differ?
o: Both passages suggest that friends should avoid difficult conversations to protect their friendships.
Passage 1 suggests lying to protect a friend is kind; Passage 2 suggests blunt honesty helps a friend most.
Passage 1 is about cheating at school, while Passage 2 is about writing music with a close friend.
Passage 1 shows the harm in covering for a friend; Passage 2 shows honest feedback works best given with care.
w: Nadia's cover story leads both girls into trouble, and Jo wishes Nadia had refused, so Passage 1 warns against covering for a friend. Sam's blunt comment hurts while his careful feedback helps, so Passage 2 is about delivering truth with care.

n.0: Both passages show that avoiding the truth or delivering it carelessly causes harm; neither recommends avoiding hard conversations.
n.1: Passage 1 shows the lie backfiring, and Passage 2 shows blunt honesty hurting Theo, so both halves misread the texts.
n.2: This contrasts the settings, not the messages the stories convey.

q:
Passage 1
One cup of water on the seedling's bed
does nothing much, the hurried gardener said.
But the girl came back with one cup every day,
and by July the vine had found its way
across the fence and up into the light,
a green thing built from mornings, small and right.

Passage 2
Researchers who study habits find that people who try to change many behaviors at once often quit within weeks. Those who start with one small action, such as a five-minute walk after breakfast, are more likely to keep going. Over months, small actions repeated daily can grow into larger routines.

Which idea do the poem and the article share?
o: Gardening is a healthy daily habit for children and teenagers.
People who change many habits at once tend to give up quickly.
Morning is the best time of day to begin a new healthy habit.
Small actions repeated over time can lead to large results.
w: In the poem, one cup of water a day grows a vine across the fence; in the article, small daily actions grow into larger routines. The genres differ, but the shared idea is the power of small repeated actions.

n.0: Gardening appears in the poem only, and neither text calls it a healthy habit for young people.
n.1: This finding appears in the article only; the poem says nothing about changing many habits.
n.2: The poem mentions mornings and the article's example is after breakfast, but neither claims morning is the best time.

q:
Passage 1
After thirty years with the fire department, Walt retired and found the days long and quiet. On a friend's advice, he began training puppies to become service dogs. Now he spends his mornings teaching them to open doors and pick up dropped keys, and he says he has not felt this useful since his last shift.

Passage 2
When her husband died, Joan stopped going out except to walk her terrier. A neighbor invited her to a community choir, and she went once, then every week. Two years later, Joan organizes the choir's concerts at local hospitals and calls Tuesday rehearsal "the best night of my week."

Which theme do both passages share?
o: A new commitment can restore purpose after a major change.
Music helps people work through grief after a death.
Retirement is harder for people who did physical work.
Pets give steady comfort to people who live on their own.
w: Walt finds purpose in training service dogs after retiring, and Joan finds it in the choir after her husband's death. Both show a new commitment filling the gap left by a major life change.

n.1: This fits Passage 2 only; Passage 1 involves no music or death.
n.2: This draws on Passage 1 only and goes beyond it; Passage 1 does not compare kinds of work.
n.3: Dogs appear in both, but that is a minor shared detail; Joan's change comes from the choir, not her terrier.

q:
Passage 1
From a school board report: A review of 30 districts that moved high school start times from 7:30 to 8:30 a.m. found that students slept an average of 40 minutes more on school nights. First-period attendance rose modestly. The board recommends adopting a similar schedule next year.

Passage 2
From a parent's letter: Every morning I watch my son stumble to the bus stop in the dark, too tired to speak. Our teenagers are being asked to learn calculus on five hours of sleep! Other districts have already pushed back the first bell. How many more exhausted years will we accept before we do the same?

Which statement best describes how the two passages relate?
o: The letter favors later start times, while the report stays neutral on the proposed change.
Both favor later start times; the report relies on data and the letter on personal experience.
The report favors later start times, while the letter questions whether they would help.
Both passages question whether early start times have any effect on student attendance.
w: The report recommends the later schedule based on a 30-district review; the parent urges the same change based on watching an exhausted son. The tones differ, but the positions agree.

n.0: The report ends by recommending the later schedule, so it is not neutral.
n.2: The letter's emotional tone is not disagreement; the parent asks the district to follow others in pushing back the first bell.
n.3: The report links later starts to better attendance, and the letter never discusses attendance.

q:
Passage 1
From a hospital administrator: Last year we ended fixed visiting hours. Families may now visit at any time, because patients with loved ones nearby report less anxiety and often understand their discharge plans better. To protect rest, we allow two visitors at a time after 9 p.m.

Passage 2
From a nurse's blog: Open visiting has helped many of my patients, and I would not go back. But on night shift, a crowded room can keep a patient awake and slow down care. Hospitals that welcome families should also set quiet hours that visitors respect.

On which point do the two authors agree?
o: Patients recover faster when visitors come during daytime hours.
Nighttime visitors should be limited to two people per patient.
Family presence helps patients, but nighttime visits need some limits.
Open visiting adds to the workload of nurses on the night shift.
w: The administrator credits family presence with less anxiety and caps night visitors at two; the nurse says open visiting has helped and calls for quiet hours. Both support families while limiting nights.

n.0: Neither passage compares daytime and nighttime visits for recovery speed.
n.1: The two-visitor rule appears in Passage 1 only; the nurse proposes quiet hours, not a number.
n.3: Slower care at night is the nurse's concern in Passage 2; the administrator does not discuss workload.

q:
Passage 1
From a second-grade teacher: Studies of young children find little link between nightly homework and better grades. Worksheets often lead to tears at the kitchen table. I now ask families for one thing: read together for twenty minutes each night.

Passage 2
From a parent: My daughter's weekly homework packet does more than review math facts. It teaches her to manage her time and finish a task without being told twice. It also shows me what she is learning, so I can help when she struggles. I hope the school keeps assigning it.

The authors disagree most about whether
o: homework improves the grades of older students
reading at home each night benefits young children
young children should be given regular homework
parents should know what children learn at school
w: The teacher has replaced homework with shared reading because of weak evidence, while the parent wants the school to keep the weekly packet. Their conflict is over assigning homework to young children.

n.0: Both passages concern young children; neither discusses older students.
n.1: The teacher recommends nightly reading, and the parent never questions it, so this is not a point of disagreement.
n.3: The parent values knowing what her child learns; the teacher does not argue against it.

q:
Passage 1
City council member Ortiz: Painted bike lanes do little when a delivery truck can park in them. Protected lanes, separated from traffic by curbs or posts, are the surest way to make cycling safe enough that families will try it. The city should build them on its three busiest streets.

Passage 2
City council member Bennett: Protected lanes cost about ten times as much per mile as paint. For the same money, we could add painted lanes across the city and lower the downtown speed limit to 20 miles per hour, which would protect cyclists on every street, not just three.

Which assumption do both council members share?
o: The city's budget cannot pay for any protected bike lanes.
Lower speed limits would reduce car traffic in the downtown area.
Protected lanes are the best choice for keeping cyclists safe.
Making streets safer for cyclists is a worthwhile goal for the city.
w: Ortiz and Bennett differ on the method, but both propose spending to protect cyclists. Neither questions the goal itself, so it is the assumption they share.

n.0: Bennett says protected lanes cost more, not that the city cannot afford any.
n.1: Bennett proposes lower speeds to protect cyclists, not to reduce traffic, and Ortiz does not mention speed.
n.2: This is Ortiz's position; Bennett argues that paint plus lower speeds would protect more cyclists.

q:
Passage 1
From a beverage industry statement: A standard can of our energy drink contains about the same amount of caffeine as a large cup of coffee. Parents who are comfortable with their teenagers drinking coffee should have no greater concern about energy drinks.

Passage 2
From a pediatrician: A single can may hold about as much caffeine as coffee, but teenagers rarely sip energy drinks slowly the way they sip hot coffee. Many drink two or three cans quickly, often during sports, and some mix them with other caffeinated products. That pattern, not the single can, is what sends teens to emergency rooms with racing hearts.

How would the author of Passage 2 most likely respond to the claim in Passage 1?
o: The comparison ignores how quickly and in what amounts teens drink them.
Teens who drink coffee face the same risks as those who drink energy drinks.
Energy drinks contain much more caffeine per can than coffee does.
The industry is correct, so parents can set aside their concerns.
w: The pediatrician grants that one can is similar to coffee but argues that the real danger is drinking several cans quickly. That response targets the industry's single-can comparison.

n.1: The pediatrician contrasts how teens drink coffee and energy drinks, so the risks are not presented as the same.
n.2: The pediatrician concedes that a can may hold about as much caffeine as coffee.
n.3: The pediatrician describes emergency room visits, which shows continued concern.

q:
Passage 1
In 1816, the French physician Rene Laennec needed to listen to a patient's heart but felt uncomfortable pressing his ear to her chest. He rolled a few sheets of paper into a tube, placed one end on her chest, and was surprised by how clearly he could hear. He later built a wooden version and called it a stethoscope.

Passage 2
Hear what you have been missing. The ClearBeat Digital Stethoscope amplifies heart and lung sounds up to 40 times and filters out room noise. Record sounds, share them with colleagues, and replay them in slow motion. Order today and receive a free carrying case.

Which statement best describes how the purposes of the passages differ?
o: Both passages mainly explain the way that a stethoscope makes sounds louder for doctors.
Passage 1 informs readers about the device's origin; Passage 2 urges readers to buy one.
Passage 1 argues for older stethoscopes; Passage 2 informs about recording heart sounds.
Passage 1 entertains with a personal story; Passage 2 explains how digital sound works.
w: Passage 1 is a short history of how the stethoscope was invented. Passage 2 is an advertisement with a call to action (Order today) and an offer, so its purpose is to persuade.

n.0: Passage 1 tells how the device was invented, and Passage 2 sells a product; neither mainly explains amplification.
n.2: Passage 1 makes no argument for older devices; it simply recounts the invention.
n.3: Passage 1 uses an anecdote, but to inform about history; and Passage 2 sells a product rather than explaining technology.

q:
Passage 1
Rural school districts struggle to hire teachers, who can often earn more in cities. A four-day school week offers something cities rarely can: a free weekday. It also saves districts money on buses and heating, though the main reason to adopt it is recruiting.

Passage 2
Two years after Pine Hollow District switched to a four-day week, student attendance had stayed about the same. Applications for open teaching jobs doubled. In a survey, many parents reported paying more for child care on the fifth day.

Which detail from Passage 2 best supports the main claim of Passage 1?
o: Student attendance stayed about the same after the switch.
Many parents reported higher child care costs on the fifth day.
Four-day weeks save districts money on buses and heating.
Applications for open teaching jobs doubled after the switch.
w: Passage 1's main claim is that a four-day week helps rural districts recruit teachers. Doubled teaching applications in Pine Hollow is direct evidence for that claim.

n.0: Stable attendance is a real finding, but it does not address teacher recruitment.
n.1: Higher child care costs are a drawback and do nothing to support the recruiting claim.
n.2: This detail comes from Passage 1, not Passage 2, and it is a side benefit rather than the main claim.

q:
Passage 1
From a rural clinic director: Since we began offering video visits, patients who once drove ninety minutes for a five-minute medication check can now do it from home. Video works well for follow-ups. Some problems, such as a new lump or chest pain, still require an in-person exam.

Passage 2
From a patient advocate: Telehealth is convenient for many patients, but many older adults in our county lack reliable internet. Insurers should pay for phone-only visits as well as video. Even then, telehealth should add to the clinic, not replace it.

Which statements would both authors most likely agree with? Select all that apply.
o: Follow-up visits work best when they are done by video.
Telehealth makes care more convenient for many patients.
Rural patients are the main users of telehealth services.
Insurers should pay for phone-only visits as well as video.
Most older adults in the county lack internet at home.
Telehealth cannot take the place of every in-person visit.
w: The director praises saved drives and the advocate calls telehealth convenient for many. The director says some problems need an in-person exam, and the advocate says telehealth should add to the clinic, not replace it.

n.0: The director says video works well for follow-ups; the advocate does not comment on follow-ups.
n.2: Neither passage compares rural patients with other users.
n.3: Only the advocate calls for phone-only coverage; the director does not address insurance.
n.4: The advocate says many older adults lack reliable internet, not most, and the director does not discuss it.

q:
Passage 1
A 2023 study of six middle schools found that students threw away about a third of the food on their lunch trays. Fruit and vegetables were discarded most often. The waste costs districts money and sends tons of food to landfills each year.

Passage 2
This fall, Riverside Middle School placed a share table near the cafeteria exit. Students leave unopened milk, packaged snacks, and whole fruit they do not want, and classmates may take them. A local food pantry collects what is left each Friday. Food waste in the cafeteria fell by about 30 percent in three months.

Which statement best describes how Passage 2 relates to Passage 1?
o: It questions the data that Passage 1 uses to describe cafeteria waste.
It narrows Passage 1's topic to the cost of school lunches.
It repeats the main claim of Passage 1 using new statistics.
It describes one approach to the problem that Passage 1 explains.
w: Passage 1 describes the problem of cafeteria food waste. Passage 2 reports one school's share table and the 30 percent drop in waste that followed, which is a response to that problem.

n.0: Passage 2 never disputes Passage 1's findings; it assumes waste is a problem worth reducing.
n.1: Passage 2 does not discuss lunch costs; it describes a program that reduces waste.
n.2: Passage 2's statistic measures the result of a solution, not the size of the problem.

q:
Passage 1
From the hospital newsletter: In this year's staff survey, 60 percent of our nurses said they would recommend Lakeside General as a place to work. That result reflects the strong teamwork and pride our nursing staff bring to every shift.

Passage 2
From a nurses' union bulletin: The same survey means that 40 percent of nurses would not recommend Lakeside as a workplace. With one in five nurses leaving each year, management should treat this number as a warning, not a reason to celebrate.

The authors disagree mainly about
o: whether nurse morale affects the quality of patient care
what the survey result shows about nurses' morale
whether the survey was conducted by the hospital itself
how many nurses said they would recommend the hospital
w: Both accept the same figure (60 percent would recommend, so 40 percent would not). The newsletter reads it as a sign of pride; the union reads it as a warning. They disagree about interpretation.

n.0: Neither passage discusses patient care.
n.2: Neither passage raises who conducted the survey.
n.3: Both use the same survey figures, so they agree about the numbers.

q:
Passage 1
From a high school teacher: This year our school began collecting phones at the front office each morning. Students pick them up at dismissal. Parents who need to reach their child during the day call the office, and we deliver the message within minutes. Since the change, I see students talking to each other at lunch, and fewer students drift off in class.

Passage 2
From a student: Taking our phones all day puts us at risk. If there is an emergency, or if my mom needs to tell me that my ride has changed, how is she supposed to reach me?

Based on Passage 1, how would its author most likely respond to the concern in Passage 2?
o: Families can still reach students through the school office.
Students should keep their phones on silent inside their bags.
Emergencies at school are too rare to plan for in a policy.
Students who need their phones may use them during lunch.
w: The teacher explains that parents call the office and messages are delivered within minutes. That arrangement directly answers the student's worry about being reached.

n.1: The teacher supports collecting phones at the office, so keeping them in bags conflicts with Passage 1.
n.2: The teacher never dismisses emergencies; Passage 1 describes a way to handle urgent messages.
n.3: Passage 1 says phones stay at the office until dismissal, so lunch use is not part of the policy.

q:
Passage 1
From a public health official: Sugary drinks are the largest single source of added sugar in American diets. When the price of a product rises, people buy less of it. A tax of two cents per ounce would lower consumption and fund school nutrition programs.

Passage 2
From a community organizer: A soda tax takes the biggest bite from families who are already stretched thin, since they spend a larger share of their income on groceries. If we want people to drink fewer sugary drinks, we should fund clean water stations in parks and nutrition classes in schools.

Which assumption do the two authors share?
o: Low-income families buy more sugary drinks than other families.
A tax is the most effective way to cut sugary drink consumption.
Lowering sugary drink consumption would benefit public health.
Nutrition classes in schools have had little effect on habits.
w: The official proposes a tax to lower consumption, and the organizer says "if we want people to drink fewer sugary drinks" and offers other methods. Both take for granted that less consumption is desirable.

n.0: The organizer says lower-income families spend a larger share of income on groceries, not that they buy more soda.
n.1: This is the official's position; the organizer rejects the tax in favor of other approaches.
n.3: The organizer recommends nutrition classes, and the official does not discuss them.

q:
Passage 1
Protect yourself while you are here. Clean your hands before you eat, after you use the bathroom, and when you enter or leave a patient's room. Rub hand sanitizer over all surfaces of your hands until they are dry, about 20 seconds. It is okay to ask your care team, "Did you clean your hands?"

Passage 2
To: All clinical staff. Hand hygiene audits on Units 4 and 5 found compliance of 71 percent in March, below our goal of 90 percent. Beginning May 1, unit managers will post monthly audit results, and units below goal will complete a refresher module.

Which statement best describes a difference between the passages?
o: Passage 1 is written for patients and visitors; Passage 2, for hospital staff.
Passage 1 gives infection data; Passage 2 gives steps for cleaning hands.
Passage 1 is written for newly hired nurses; Passage 2, for the hospital's unit managers.
Passage 1 gives directions in the second person; Passage 2 tells a nurse's personal story.
w: Passage 1 speaks to "you" while you are here and invites you to ask your care team, so its audience is patients and visitors. Passage 2 is a memo addressed to all clinical staff about audit results.

n.1: This reverses the passages: Passage 1 gives the steps, and Passage 2 gives audit data.
n.2: Passage 1 invites readers to ask their care team, so it addresses patients and visitors; Passage 2 goes to all clinical staff, not just managers.
n.3: Passage 1 does address "you," but Passage 2 is a memo reporting audit data and a new policy, not a personal story.

q:
(1) Every year, the Ridgeview public pool opens on Memorial Day and closes on Labor Day. (2) Yet the hottest weeks in our town now often arrive in September, when the pool sits empty behind a locked gate. (3) Ridgeview should keep the pool open through the end of September. (4) Last year, the high temperature topped 90 °F on eleven September days. (5) Some council members worry about the cost of lifeguards once college students return to school. (6) But the high school swim team has offered certified lifeguards on weekends, and extra admission fees would cover weekday staff.

Which sentence states the author's main claim?
o: Sentence 3
Sentence 2
Sentence 4
Sentence 6
w: Sentence 3 states the position the whole letter defends: keep the pool open through September. The other sentences give reasons, evidence, an objection, and a response to it.

n.1: Sentence 2 is a reason for the claim (the hot weeks have shifted), not the position itself.
n.2: Sentence 4 is evidence, a statistic supporting the reason in Sentence 2.
n.3: Sentence 6 is a rebuttal that answers the cost objection raised in Sentence 5.

q:
Every high school graduate in our state should leave knowing how to perform CPR. When a person's heart stops outside a hospital, the chance of survival drops with each minute before chest compressions begin, and many of these emergencies happen at home, in front of family members. Critics say schools already have too little time for core subjects. Yet hands-only CPR can be taught in a single 30-minute session, often during an existing health class. Several states already require the lesson, and none has reported that it crowded out other learning.

The sentence "Critics say schools already have too little time for core subjects" mainly serves to
o: concede that the author's proposal should wait until a later year
present an opposing view that the author then goes on to answer
give evidence that CPR training improves survival after cardiac arrest
state the main claim that the author supports throughout the passage
w: The sentence reports what critics say, and the next sentence begins "Yet" and answers it (the lesson takes one 30-minute session). It introduces a counterclaim that the author rebuts.

n.0: The author does not concede the point; the next sentence rejects it.
n.2: The survival evidence is in the second sentence; this sentence is about class time.
n.3: The main claim is the first sentence: every graduate should know CPR. This sentence presents a view that challenges it.

q:
Laundry detergent pods should be sold in opaque, child-resistant containers. Dr. Alicia Moreno, who has directed the county poison control center for fifteen years, says the brightly colored pods look like candy to toddlers. "In my experience, most of these calls involve children under three who found a container on a low shelf," she explains. Moreno adds that a container a toddler cannot see into or open would prevent many of the calls her staff answers each week. Manufacturers argue that warning labels are enough, but Moreno points out that toddlers cannot read.

Which type of evidence does the author mainly use to support the claim?
o: A comparison with another state's packaging laws
Testimony from an expert who works in the field
A personal story about one family's emergency
Statistics from a controlled study of poisoning cases
w: Nearly every supporting sentence reports what Dr. Moreno, the long-time poison control director, says from her professional experience. That is expert testimony.

n.0: No other state or law is mentioned.
n.2: No individual family's story is told; Moreno speaks in general terms about the calls her center receives.
n.3: The passage gives no study and no numbers; "most of these calls" is Moreno's experience, not statistical data.

q:
Last winter, a volunteer found a gray terrier curled in a roadside ditch, too weak to lift his head. We named him Biscuit. For three weeks, our staff fed him by hand every four hours and wrapped him in warm towels while he shivered through the nights. This morning, Biscuit trotted out the front door with his new family, tail wagging. Our shelter cares for about 400 animals a year. Every Biscuit begins with a donor like you. Please give today.

The author mainly tries to persuade readers by appealing to their
o: sense of logic, through data on the shelter's yearly costs
trust, through the shelter director's professional credentials
sense of duty, by comparing the shelter with other shelters
emotions, through a vivid story about a single rescued dog
w: Most of the letter tells Biscuit's story in moving detail (too weak to lift his head, shivering, tail wagging) before asking for money. That is mainly an appeal to emotion (pathos).

n.0: One figure appears (about 400 animals a year), but no cost data, and the story carries the appeal.
n.1: The letter never names its author's role or credentials.
n.2: No other shelters are mentioned.

q:
(1) The Eastside branch library should stay open until 9 p.m. on weeknights instead of closing at 6. (2) Many adults in our neighborhood work until 5:30 and cannot reach the branch before it closes. (3) When the branch tested evening hours last fall, it checked out 1,800 more items in two months. (4) Some board members say the extra hours would cost too much in staff pay. (5) However, the test was staffed by volunteers from the Friends of the Library, who have offered to continue. (6) Our neighbors deserve a library they can actually use.

Which sentence is a rebuttal?
o: Sentence 5
Sentence 3
Sentence 2
Sentence 4
w: Sentence 4 raises an objection (staff costs). Sentence 5, beginning with "However," answers that objection by noting volunteers covered the test and have offered to continue. A rebuttal is a response to a counterclaim.

n.1: Sentence 3 is evidence from the trial period supporting the claim.
n.2: Sentence 2 is a reason supporting the claim; it does not answer an objection.
n.3: Sentence 4 is the counterclaim itself, the objection that Sentence 5 rebuts.

q:
Our county should require bicycle helmets for riders under 16. Head injuries are the leading cause of serious harm in bicycle crashes, and a helmet that fits correctly greatly lowers the risk of a brain injury. In the past three years, the county trauma center treated 46 children for head injuries from bike crashes, and only 5 of them had been wearing helmets. Helmets now cost as little as $15, and the fire department gives them away free at every spring safety fair. A helmet rule would protect our children at little cost to families.

Which element of a complete argument is missing from the passage?
o: A clear claim that the author wants readers to accept
A reason explaining why the claim deserves support
A response to an objection that opponents might raise
Evidence that supports the reasons behind the claim
w: The passage states a claim, gives reasons (head injuries, low cost), and supports them with evidence (46 children, 5 in helmets; $15 helmets). It never raises or answers an opposing view, such as concerns about enforcement or personal choice.

n.0: The first sentence states the claim directly: require helmets for riders under 16.
n.1: The passage gives reasons: helmets lower brain injury risk and cost families little.
n.3: The trauma center figures and the helmet prices are evidence.

q:
(1) Our city should plant 5,000 street trees over the next five years. (2) A 2021 study by the state forestry office found that tree-lined blocks in our city were up to 9 °F cooler on summer afternoons than nearby blocks without trees. (3) Shade is a public health issue, not just a matter of looks. (4) During last July's heat wave, the county hospital treated 140 people for heat illness, most of them from neighborhoods with few trees. (5) Trees also make a neighborhood more pleasant for walking. (6) The council should fund the plan in this year's budget.

Which sentences present evidence rather than a claim or reason? Select all that apply.
o: Sentence 5
Sentence 4
Sentence 6
Sentence 2
Sentence 1
Sentence 3
w: Sentence 2 reports a study's measured temperature difference, and Sentence 4 reports hospital figures from a heat wave. Both are verifiable facts offered to support the claim.

n.0: Sentence 5 is an additional reason based on opinion; no evidence backs it up.
n.2: Sentence 6 is a call to action that restates the claim.
n.4: Sentence 1 is the main claim: what the author wants the city to do.
n.5: Sentence 3 is a reason stated as the author's judgment; the evidence for it comes in Sentence 4.

q:
Last school year, three children were struck by cars while walking to Garfield Elementary. All three accidents happened at the Elm Street and Fourth Avenue intersections, the only crossings near the school without an adult crossing guard. The school board should hire two more crossing guards before classes start in August. The cost, about $18,000 a year, is small compared with the medical bills from even one serious injury.

Which assumption links the author's evidence to the claim?
o: Crossing guards lower the chance that children are struck at intersections.
The number of children walking to Garfield will rise in the coming school year.
Garfield's guarded crossings carry less car traffic than Elm Street and Fourth Avenue.
Drivers near Garfield are less careful than drivers in other parts of town.
w: The evidence is that accidents happened at crossings without guards; the claim is that guards should be hired. The argument works only if guards actually make those crossings safer for children.

n.1: The argument rests on last year's accidents at unguarded crossings; it does not depend on more children walking.
n.2: Lighter traffic at the guarded crossings would be another explanation for where the accidents happened, so it would weaken the argument rather than link it.
n.3: The argument compares crossings with and without guards, not drivers in different parts of town.

q:
When my grandmother broke her hip, the nearest rehabilitation center was two hours away, and our family could visit only on Sundays. Rural counties like ours need small rehab units attached to local hospitals. Patients recover better when family members can visit often, according to a review of 22 studies on stroke and hip-fracture recovery. Some health officials argue that small units cannot afford specialized staff. But traveling therapists already rotate among rural hospitals in neighboring counties, and the state could fund the same model here. Write to your state representative this week.

Which statement best describes how the argument is organized?
o: A story introduces a claim, which is supported, challenged, and then defended.
A claim is stated, and the author changes position after weighing an objection.
A problem is described in detail, and the author declines to propose a remedy.
Two opposing views receive equal weight, and readers are left to decide.
w: The grandmother's story leads to the claim (rural rehab units), followed by evidence (the 22-study review), an objection (staffing costs), a rebuttal (traveling therapists), and a call to action.

n.1: The author answers the objection with traveling therapists and keeps the original position.
n.2: The author proposes rehab units and a state-funded therapist model.
n.3: The author clearly takes one side and urges readers to act on it.

q:
Supporters of the proposed ban on plastic grocery bags claim it will cut litter in our parks in half. The evidence from cities that have tried such bans suggests a smaller effect: studies in three comparable cities found that plastic bag litter fell, but overall park litter dropped by about 20 percent. Even so, I will vote for the ban. A 20 percent drop is real progress, the cost to shoppers is a reusable bag, and our parks crew spends hundreds of hours a year picking up plastic.

Which statement best expresses the author's own position?
o: The ban is worth adopting even if its effect is smaller than claimed.
The ban will cut park litter in half, as its supporters have claimed.
The ban should be rejected because its effect on park litter is modest.
The city should study the ban for another year before it votes on it.
w: The author doubts the supporters' 50 percent claim, citing a drop of about 20 percent, but says "Even so, I will vote for the ban" because that drop is real progress.

n.1: This is the supporters' claim, which the author reports and then questions.
n.2: The author calls the effect modest but supports the ban anyway.
n.3: The author does not call for more study and states a plan to vote for the ban.

q:
Companies should encourage walking meetings for small-group brainstorming. Many offices book every conference room by 9 a.m., and walking meetings need no reserved space. In a university study, participants came up with about 60 percent more creative uses for everyday objects while walking than while sitting. Walking also burns more calories than sitting at a conference table, which may matter to employees who spend most of the day at a desk. "I like getting fresh air in the middle of the day," said one employee at a firm that tried the idea.

Which sentence from the passage best supports the author's main claim?
o: In a university study, participants came up with about 60 percent more creative uses for everyday objects while walking.
"I like getting fresh air in the middle of the day," said one employee at a firm that tried the idea.
Many offices book every conference room by 9 a.m., and walking meetings need no reserved space.
Walking also burns more calories than sitting at a conference table, which may matter to employees who spend most of the day at a desk.
w: Step 1: the main claim is about brainstorming, a creative task. Step 2: the study showing about 60 percent more creative ideas while walking supports that specific claim most directly.

n.1: One employee's preference is a weak anecdote and concerns fresh air, not idea generation.
n.2: Room shortages explain a convenience, not why walking meetings improve brainstorming.
n.3: Calories relate to health, a side benefit rather than the brainstorming claim.

q:
As a firefighter for 22 years, I have been inside hundreds of homes after a fire, and I have learned which ones families walk out of. Our city should require landlords to install working smoke alarms in every bedroom of every rental unit. Smoke alarms give sleeping families the minutes they need to escape. The cost to a landlord is about $25 per alarm. Tenants should not have to buy their own safety.

In the first sentence, the author mainly uses which type of appeal?
o: Counterclaim, by stating a view the author rejects
Pathos, by describing a frightening fire in detail
Logos, by citing statistics on deaths in rental fires
Ethos, by establishing experience with the topic
w: The first sentence tells readers the author has 22 years of firefighting experience inside hundreds of homes. That builds credibility, an appeal to ethos.

n.0: The sentence presents no opposing view; it supports the author's authority.
n.1: The sentence describes the author's experience, not a vivid scene of a particular fire.
n.2: The first sentence gives no statistics; the only figure in the passage is the alarm cost, later.

q:
At Tuesday's school board meeting, parent Linda Cho proposed adding a second recess period for grades 1 through 3. She summarized several studies linking short breaks for play with better attention in class. Board member Gary Platt responded: "Ms. Cho has no teaching degree, and her own children have been sent to the principal's office more than once. Why should this board take advice on student behavior from her?" The board then moved to the next item on the agenda without discussing the studies.

Which fallacy does Platt's response contain?
o: Red herring
Appeal to emotion
Ad hominem
Straw man
w: Platt attacks Cho's lack of a degree and her children's behavior instead of the studies she presented. Rejecting an argument because of who made it is an ad hominem fallacy.

n.0: A red herring shifts to an unrelated topic; Platt's response is aimed squarely at Cho herself, which is the defining feature of ad hominem.
n.1: Platt does not try to stir feelings about recess or children; he discredits the speaker.
n.3: A straw man distorts the opponent's position; Platt never restates Cho's proposal at all.

q:
Council member Reyes has proposed closing two blocks of Main Street to cars on Saturday mornings from May through September so that a farmers market can set up. Her opponent responded: "Reyes wants to ban cars from downtown. If she had her way, delivery trucks could not reach our stores, and shoppers who drive would have nowhere to go. I cannot support a plan that shuts down our business district."

Which statement best describes the flaw in the opponent's response?
o: It claims the plan is good or bad based on how many people favor it.
It attacks an exaggerated version of the plan instead of the real one.
It attacks Reyes's character instead of discussing her proposal.
It presents two choices as the only ones when others exist.
w: Reyes proposed closing two blocks on summer Saturday mornings, but the opponent describes a ban on cars downtown and argues against that. Misrepresenting a position to make it easier to attack is a straw man.

n.0: The response never mentions public opinion or popularity.
n.2: The opponent criticizes a (distorted) plan, not Reyes's character, so this is not ad hominem.
n.3: The response does not reduce the issue to two options; it rejects a misdescribed plan.

q:
Letter to the student newspaper: The faculty senate is considering a policy that would let students retake one failed exam per course. This would be a mistake. If students know they can retake an exam, they will stop studying for first attempts. Soon nearly every exam will be taken twice, instructors will spend their time writing makeup tests instead of teaching, and within a few years employers will stop taking our degrees seriously.

Which fallacy does the letter contain?
o: Circular reasoning
Post hoc
Hasty generalization
Slippery slope
