w: The writer claims one small policy will set off a chain of worsening results (no studying, every exam taken twice, worthless degrees) without evidence for each step. That is a slippery slope.

n.0: Circular reasoning restates its conclusion as its reason; the letter gives a (weak) chain of causes.
n.1: Post hoc claims a past event caused a later one because it came first; the letter predicts future consequences instead.
n.2: A hasty generalization draws a broad conclusion from a few examples; the letter offers no examples.

q:
In January, the cafeteria at Mercy Valley Hospital switched to a new coffee supplier. In February, the number of sick days taken by staff fell by 15 percent compared with January. The cafeteria manager announced that the new coffee is clearly better for staff health and asked the newsletter editor to feature it in the next issue. The manager did not mention that January had been the peak of the local flu season.

Which statement best describes the flaw in the manager's reasoning?
o: It rejects an opposing view by attacking the people who hold that view.
It draws a conclusion about every hospital from one hospital's records.
It assumes that its conclusion is true in order to prove that conclusion.
It assumes that because one event came first, it caused the second one.
w: Sick days fell after the coffee changed, so the manager concludes the coffee caused the drop. That is post hoc reasoning, and the end of flu season is a more likely explanation.

n.0: The manager does not respond to any opponent, so there is no personal attack.
n.1: The manager draws a conclusion about this hospital's staff, not about every hospital.
n.2: The manager offers a reason (fewer sick days) that is separate from the conclusion; the flaw is the causal leap.

q:
At a town meeting, the director of the Hillside Community Clinic said, "Our budget is $40,000 short this year. Either we close the clinic on Saturdays, or we raise the fee for every visit by $20. There is no other way to balance the books." Several residents pointed out that the clinic had not yet applied for a state grant, asked local businesses for support, or reviewed its supply costs.

Which fallacy does the director's statement contain?
o: Straw man
Slippery slope
Red herring
False dilemma
w: The director presents two options as the only choices, while residents name several others (a grant, business support, lower supply costs). Ignoring other options is a false dilemma.

n.0: A straw man misrepresents an opponent's position; the director does not describe anyone else's view.
n.1: A slippery slope predicts a chain of worsening events; the director predicts no chain.
n.2: A red herring switches to an unrelated topic; the director stays on the budget.

q:
In a television commercial, a famous Olympic swimmer holds up a bottle of DreamEase, a sleep supplement. "I have won six gold medals," she says, "and I trust DreamEase to help me sleep before every race. If it works for a champion, it will work for you." The commercial shows her diving into a pool as the product name appears on screen. It does not mention any research on the supplement or its ingredients.

Which statement best describes the main weakness of the commercial's argument?
o: It criticizes rival supplements instead of describing its own product.
It claims the product works because many people already use it.
It presents two choices for better sleep when many others are available.
It relies on a celebrity whose expertise has no bearing on the product.
w: The swimmer's medals show athletic skill, not knowledge of sleep or supplements, and no research is offered. Using an irrelevant authority as proof is an appeal to false authority.

n.0: No rival products are mentioned.
n.1: The commercial relies on one famous person, not on how many people use the product, so it is not a bandwagon appeal.
n.2: The commercial does not frame a choice between two options.

q:
After her first two evening shifts at the new urgent care center, Brianna told her roommate, "Both nights, the waiting room was nearly empty by 9 p.m. People in this town obviously don't use urgent care in the evening. The center should close at 8 and save money on staff." The center had opened the week before, during a holiday, when many families were out of town.

Which fallacy does Brianna's reasoning contain?
o: Appeal to tradition
Post hoc
Circular reasoning
Hasty generalization
w: Brianna draws a broad conclusion about the whole town's habits from two nights, and those nights fell during an unusual holiday week. That is a hasty generalization from too few, unrepresentative examples.

n.0: She makes no appeal to how things have always been done; the center is brand new.
n.1: Brianna does not claim that one event caused a later one; she generalizes from a small sample.
n.2: Her conclusion rests on observations, not on a restatement of itself; the problem is the tiny sample.

q:
From a website that reviews nutrition books: "The Greenleaf Diet Guide is the most reliable guide on the market. We know it can be trusted because it is the most dependable source of diet advice available today. Readers who want accurate information should choose it over every other guide." The review does not name the guide's author, describe the author's training, or list any of the sources the guide uses.

Which statement best describes the flaw in the review's reasoning?
o: It attacks the authors of other guides instead of judging their advice.
It gives a reason for trusting the guide that restates its own claim.
It trusts the guide because a well-known person has recommended it.
It judges the guide by the number of readers who have bought a copy.
w: "Most reliable" is supported only by "most dependable," which says the same thing in other words. The conclusion is used as its own premise, which is circular reasoning.

n.0: Other guides are mentioned only in passing; their authors are not attacked.
n.2: No person is named as recommending the guide, so this is not an appeal to authority.
n.3: The review never mentions sales or popularity.

q:
At a public meeting, several residents asked the hospital's spokesperson why parking fees in the visitor garage had doubled this year. The spokesperson replied, "I understand your concern. But let me tell you about our new rooftop garden, which gives patients a peaceful place to recover. It was funded by donors and has been praised by patients and their families." She then invited the next question, and the parking fees were not discussed again.

Which fallacy does the spokesperson's reply contain?
o: Red herring
Ad hominem
Straw man
Bandwagon
w: The question was about parking fees, and the spokesperson shifts attention to the rooftop garden, a topic unrelated to the fees. Distracting from the issue with an irrelevant topic is a red herring.

n.1: The spokesperson does not attack the residents who asked the question.
n.2: A straw man restates the opponent's view in a distorted form; the spokesperson does not restate the residents' concern at all.
n.3: The reply mentions praise for the garden but does not argue that fees are fair because many people agree.

q:
A district analysis found that the high schools with the most vending machines also had the lowest average test scores. At the next meeting, a board member said, "Vending machines are hurting our students' learning. If we remove them, test scores will rise." The same analysis showed that the schools with more vending machines were also larger and had fewer counselors per student, but the board member did not mention those findings.

Which statement best describes the flaw in the board member's reasoning?
o: It bases a broad conclusion on the experience of a single high school.
It rejects the district's analysis because of the people who wrote it.
It predicts that one small change will lead to a series of disasters.
It treats a link between two things as proof that one causes the other.
w: Vending machines and low scores occur together, but the board member assumes the machines cause the scores, even though school size and counselor numbers also differ. That treats correlation as causation.

n.0: The analysis covered several high schools, so the problem is not a single example.
n.1: The board member uses the analysis rather than rejecting it, and no one is attacked.
n.2: The board member predicts a benefit from one change, not a chain of disasters.

q:
Several nurses on 4 West have proposed moving the morning shift change from 7:00 to 6:30 a.m. so that handoff reports finish before the 7:00 medications are due. They point out that nurses now give morning medications late on most days. The unit manager rejected the idea: "Shift change has been at 7:00 since this hospital opened in 1974. It has worked for fifty years, and I see no reason to change it now."

Which fallacy does the manager's response contain?
o: Hasty generalization
False dilemma
Bandwagon
Appeal to tradition
w: The manager defends the 7:00 shift change because it has been done that way since 1974, without answering the nurses' point about late medications. Arguing that something is right because it is long-standing is an appeal to tradition.

n.0: The manager does not generalize from a few examples.
n.1: The manager does not reduce the issue to two options.
n.2: Bandwagon appeals to what many people currently do or believe; the manager appeals to history.

q:
Letter to the editor: Nearly everyone I know in Maple Heights has already signed the petition against the new cell tower on Birch Road, so the council should listen to the community and reject it. Think about your children sleeping a few hundred feet from that tower every single night. Do you really want to gamble with their health? Vote no before it is too late.

Which fallacies does the letter contain? Select all that apply.
o: Ad hominem
Straw man
Bandwagon
Appeal to false authority
Circular reasoning
Appeal to fear
w: "Nearly everyone I know has signed" argues from popularity (bandwagon). The image of children sleeping near the tower and "gamble with their health" try to frighten readers without any evidence of harm (appeal to fear).

n.0: The letter does not attack any person who supports the tower.
n.1: The letter never states or distorts an opponent's position.
n.3: No expert or celebrity is cited.
n.4: The letter's reasons (the petition, fear for children) are separate from its conclusion, even though they are weak.

q:
Two years ago, the city of Fairview replaced the old orange streetlights on its major roads with bright white LED lights. In the year after the change, car crashes between sunset and sunrise fell by 18 percent. Council member Diaz argues that the brighter lights made cars and pedestrians easier to see and caused the drop. She now wants to install the same lights on every residential street.

Which of the following, if true, would most weaken Diaz's argument?
o: The LED lights cost the city less to run each year than the old streetlights did.
That same year, the city lowered speed limits on the roads with the most crashes.
Daytime crashes on the same roads stayed about the same during that year.
Residents say that the new lights make the streets look brighter and feel safer.
w: Lower speed limits on the same roads in the same year offer another explanation for fewer crashes. If something else changed at the same time, the drop cannot be credited to the lights alone.

n.0: Operating cost is a separate benefit; it says nothing about whether the lights reduced crashes.
n.2: Steady daytime crashes suggest the drop was specific to dark hours, which supports the lighting explanation.
n.3: Residents' impressions do not challenge the causal claim and, if anything, are loosely consistent with it.

q:
A health blogger claims that a 20-minute nap in mid-afternoon makes office workers more alert for the rest of the day. As evidence, she cites a poll of 300 of her readers: 82 percent of those who nap regularly said they feel sharper after a nap. She recommends that employers set aside quiet rooms where workers can sleep during their afternoon breaks.

Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the blogger's claim?
o: Most of the blogger's readers who nap regularly say they enjoy taking naps.
Several famous inventors and leaders were known to take short daytime naps.
Workers who nap for an hour or more often report feeling groggy after waking.
Workers chosen at random to nap scored higher on alertness tests than non-nappers.
w: The blogger's evidence is a self-selected poll of how readers feel. A study that randomly assigns workers to nap and measures alertness with tests provides stronger, controlled evidence for the same claim.

n.0: Enjoying naps is not the same as being more alert, so this adds nothing to the claim.
n.1: Famous examples are anecdotes, not evidence that naps raise alertness in office workers.
n.2: This concerns long naps, not the 20-minute naps in the claim, and it does not show any benefit.

q:
From a parent's letter to the school board: Students who live on the north side of Grant County deserve a second bus route. The current route starts at the county line and winds through three subdivisions before reaching the high school. My son leaves home at 6:10 a.m. for an 8:00 bell. A second route would let north-side students sleep later and arrive ready to learn.

Which additional piece of evidence would most directly support the parent's claim?
o: The parent's son must wake up at 5:30 a.m. to catch the bus on time.
North-side students now spend an average of 70 minutes on the bus each way.
South-side students now spend an average of 25 minutes on the bus each way.
A district survey found that most students prefer riding the bus to being driven.
w: The claim rests on north-side students spending too long getting to school. An average ride time of 70 minutes each way for that group is relevant and goes beyond one family's experience.

n.0: This adds one more detail about the same family; it shows nothing about north-side students as a group.
n.2: This describes a different route; without north-side ride times, it does not show the north-side route is too long.
n.3: Student preferences about riding are not evidence that the current route takes too long.

q:
From a clinic manager's memo: Starting next month, I recommend that we ask every patient with high blood pressure to use the PulseTrack phone app to log their readings. My neighbor started using PulseTrack in March. She checks her pressure every morning, and her readings are the best they have been in years. The app is free and easy to set up, so there is no reason to wait.

Which statement best evaluates the evidence in the memo?
o: It is strong, because the neighbor's readings improved after she began using the app.
It is irrelevant, because a phone app has no connection to blood pressure readings.
It is insufficient, because one person's results cannot show the app helps most patients.
It is credible, because the manager watched the neighbor's results firsthand each day.
w: The only evidence is one neighbor's experience. It is relevant, but a single anecdote is not enough to show that the app would help a clinic's whole patient population.

n.0: Improvement after starting the app is one case and may have other causes; it does not make the evidence strong.
n.1: The app logs blood pressure readings, so the evidence is related to the claim; the problem is its amount.
n.3: The memo does not say the manager observed daily results, and even firsthand observation of one person is too little evidence.

q:
A dental hygiene student is writing a report on BrightWhite, a new whitening toothpaste. The company's website claims that the toothpaste is "safe for daily use on tooth enamel." The student wants to cite evidence on this question that her instructor will accept as trustworthy. Her instructor has told the class that a source's funding, expertise, and review process all affect how much weight its evidence deserves. She has found four possible sources.

Which source would provide the most credible evidence about the toothpaste's safety for enamel?
o: Online reviews from customers who used the toothpaste for a year
A video from a popular actress who says the product worked for her
A study designed, funded, and published by the toothpaste company
An independent lab study published in a peer-reviewed dental journal
w: An independent study that passed peer review has no stake in the product and was checked by other experts, so it is the most credible evidence on safety.

n.0: Customer reviews are anecdotal and cannot measure enamel damage.
n.1: An actress is not a dental expert; her endorsement is an appeal to false authority.
n.2: The company has a financial interest in a favorable result, a conflict of interest that lowers credibility.

q:
This year, Monroe Elementary began serving free breakfast in the cafeteria from 7:30 to 7:55 a.m. The principal reports that students who ate the school breakfast at least three times a week missed an average of 4 days of school, while students who did not eat it missed an average of 9 days. She concludes that the breakfast program improves attendance and plans to ask the district to expand it.

Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the principal's conclusion?
o: Students driven to school arrive in time for breakfast, but most bus riders arrive after it ends.
The breakfast program serves whole-grain cereal, low-fat milk, and fresh fruit to students each morning.
Teachers report that students who eat the school breakfast are less restless during morning classes.
Attendance improved most among the students who ate breakfast at school on every single school day.
w: If breakfast eaters are mostly students who are driven to school, a difference in families or transportation, rather than the breakfast, could explain the attendance gap. An alternative explanation weakens a causal conclusion.

n.1: The menu describes the program but does not affect whether it caused better attendance.
n.2: This supports a different benefit (behavior) and does not undercut the attendance claim.
n.3: More breakfast linked to more improvement is a dose pattern that supports the principal's conclusion.

q:
In January, Unit 6 at Bayside Hospital installed foam hand sanitizer stations at the door of every patient room, replacing the wall-mounted gel dispensers that had hung near the nurses' station. Over the next six months, the unit's rate of hospital-acquired infections fell by about a third. The infection control nurse argues that the new stations caused the drop and wants them installed on every unit in the hospital.

Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the nurse's argument?
o: Staff on Unit 6 said that the new stations were convenient and easy to use.
The stations were placed at the door of each patient room on Unit 6.
Infection rates on similar units without the new stations did not change.
The new stations cost less to buy and refill than the old wall-mounted dispensers.
w: If similar units without the stations saw no change over the same months, a hospital-wide cause (such as a season or new policy) becomes less likely, which supports the stations as the cause.

n.0: Convenience suggests staff might use them, but it does not show that infections fell because of them.
n.1: This repeats a detail already given in the passage, so it adds no new support.
n.3: Cost is a reason to buy the stations, not evidence that they reduced infections.

q:
The town of Kellerton opened a skate park near downtown last spring. In the twelve months that followed, police reports of vandalism downtown fell by 25 percent. The year before, downtown business owners had complained about broken windows and graffiti on at least a dozen buildings. The mayor says the skate park gave teenagers a place to go and caused the drop, and she wants to build a second park on the east side.

Which of the following, if true, would weaken the mayor's argument? Select all that apply.
o: The skate park cost less to build than the town had budgeted.
Vandalism reports fell by a similar amount in nearby towns without skate parks.
That spring, police began counting several incidents at one site as one report.
The town installed security cameras downtown in the same year.
Downtown business owners say the area has felt safer at night since the park opened.
Teenagers make up most of the skate park's daily visitors, especially after school.
w: Cameras offer another cause, a similar regional drop suggests a trend unrelated to the park, and a change in how reports are counted could lower the numbers without any real change in vandalism. Each gives a reason to doubt the park caused the drop.

n.0: Building cost has no bearing on whether the park reduced vandalism.
n.4: Owners feeling safer is loosely consistent with the mayor's claim and does not offer another cause.
n.5: Teens using the park fits the mayor's explanation and does not weaken it.

q:
From a supplement company's website: MemoryMax sharpens your memory in just two weeks! In a study by a university lab, 12 adults took MemoryMax every morning for 14 days. At the end of the study, they recalled more words from a list than they had on the first day. No other group was tested. Order now and see the difference for yourself.

Which statement best evaluates the study described on the website?
o: It is unreliable because it was carried out by a university lab instead of the company.
It is sufficient to prove the claim because it measured memory directly over time.
It is relevant to the claim but too limited to establish that the product works.
It is irrelevant to the claim because it measured word recall rather than memory.
w: The study does test memory, so it is relevant. But 12 people, two weeks, and no comparison group cannot rule out practice effects (people get better at the same task with repetition), so it is not sufficient.

n.0: Independent testing usually adds credibility; the weakness is the study's size and design.
n.1: With no comparison group, the improvement could come from practice; measuring memory does not make the study sufficient.
n.3: Recalling words from a list is a memory measure, so the study is relevant.

q:
From a nurses' council proposal: Night-shift nurses on our medical units often skip their meal breaks to keep up with patient call lights. Fatigue and hunger make it harder to concentrate during the early morning medication pass. We propose that every night-shift nurse take a protected, uninterrupted 30-minute meal break, with a float nurse covering patients. We believe this change will reduce medication errors on night shift.

Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the proposal's argument?
o: Many nurses say that the meal break is the most welcome part of a long night shift.
On a unit that tested protected breaks, night-shift medication errors fell by a fifth.
Medication errors are reported more often on night shifts than on day shifts.
Night-shift nurses who take uninterrupted breaks will make fewer errors with medications.
w: A trial showing fewer night-shift errors after protected breaks were introduced is new evidence that links the proposed change to the predicted result.

n.0: Nurses' liking for breaks says nothing about medication errors.
n.2: This shows that night errors are a problem but not that protected breaks would reduce them.
n.3: This simply restates the proposal's conclusion; repeating a claim does not add support for it.

q:
From a district newsletter: Students who used the MathBoost tutoring app for at least 30 minutes a week raised their end-of-semester test scores by an average of 12 points. Students who did not use the app raised their scores by an average of 4 points. MathBoost clearly helps students learn math, and the district should buy licenses for every middle school next year.

Which of the following, if true, would most seriously challenge the claim that the app helps students learn math?
o: Some students in the study used the app for more than two hours each week.
MathBoost would cost the district about $12 per student for each school year.
Most app users were in honors classes that covered more of the tested material.
Students who used the app said they enjoyed its game-style practice lessons.
w: Step 1: the claim is that the app caused the larger score gains. Step 2: if most app users were in honors classes that covered more tested material, the class, not the app, could explain the gap.

n.0: Heavy use by some students does not offer another explanation for the score difference.
n.1: Cost bears on whether to buy the app, not on whether it helps students learn.
n.3: Enjoyment is not evidence for or against learning gains.

q:
For a child development class, Tyler wrote a report arguing that parents should limit preschoolers' screen time to two hours a day. His only source is a 1999 pamphlet from a parenting group, printed before most families owned smartphones or tablets. The pamphlet discusses television viewing and recommends the two-hour limit. Tyler did not check whether the group or any health agency has updated its advice since then.

What is the main weakness of the evidence Tyler uses?
o: It is unrelated to the subject of screen time for preschool children.
It comes from a source with a financial interest in the advice it gives.
It is too dated for a topic on which guidance may have since changed.
It is a personal story about one child rather than general guidance.
w: The pamphlet is from 1999, before smartphones and tablets were common, and Tyler never checked for updated advice. For a fast-changing topic, an old source lacks currency.

n.0: The pamphlet addresses children's screen viewing, so it is related to the topic.
n.1: The passage gives no sign that the parenting group profits from its advice.
n.3: The pamphlet offers a general recommendation, not one child's story.

q:
Keisha is writing a history paper on how the 1918 influenza pandemic affected her hometown of Clearwater. The county historical society lets her view its collection, and the reference librarian at the public library suggests several more items. She wants at least one source that comes directly from someone who lived through the outbreak in Clearwater, so she can quote that person's own observations.

Which source should Keisha use for this purpose?
o: A documentary film in which historians discuss the pandemic's effects
A 2010 book by a historian about the pandemic in small American towns
An encyclopedia entry that summarizes the 1918 influenza pandemic
A letter written in October 1918 by a Clearwater nurse to her sister
w: A letter written by a Clearwater nurse during the outbreak is a primary source: a firsthand account created at the time by someone who witnessed the events.

n.0: A documentary built on historians' commentary analyzes events after the fact, so it is secondary.
n.1: A historian's book written about 90 years later interprets earlier sources, so it is secondary.
n.2: An encyclopedia compiles and summarizes information from other sources, so it is tertiary.

q:
For a pharmacology class, Daniel is gathering sources on a common blood pressure medication. He has found four items in the college library's databases. His instructor asks students to label each source as primary, secondary, or tertiary and reminds them that the label depends on what a source does with information, not on where it is published or how technical it sounds.

Which of Daniel's sources is a secondary source?
o: A journal article reporting a clinical trial the authors ran on the drug
The de-identified records of patients who took part in a drug trial
A review article summarizing the findings of 40 studies on the drug
A pharmacology dictionary that defines the drug class in one entry
w: A review article analyzes and summarizes research that others conducted, which makes it a secondary source.

n.0: An article in which researchers report their own original trial is a primary source.
n.1: Patient records are raw data created during the study, so they are primary.
n.3: A dictionary compiles brief information from other sources, so it is tertiary.

q:
For a nursing history assignment, Jordan chose a 1998 biography of Ada Whitfield, a nurse who opened her county's first public health clinic in 1912. The author, a historian, spent ten years studying Whitfield's clinic records, newspaper notices, and letters written by people who knew her, and the book quotes many of these documents. Jordan labeled the biography a primary source in his bibliography.

Why is Jordan's label incorrect?
o: The biography is tertiary because it covers Whitfield's entire life and career.
The biography was published long after Whitfield's death, so it cannot be primary.
The author did not live these events and interprets them from records.
The book quotes letters and notices instead of reporting the author's own views.
w: A biography is a secondary source because its author did not experience the events but interprets primary sources such as clinic records, newspaper notices, and letters.

n.0: Tertiary sources compile brief summaries (encyclopedias, almanacs); a researched biography is secondary.
n.1: Date alone does not decide the category; a memoir written decades later is still primary. What matters is that the author interprets others' records.
n.3: Quoting primary documents does not make a book primary, and the author does offer interpretation.

q:
Amara is preparing a presentation on childhood asthma rates in her state. Her teacher wants students to include one example of each type of source in their bibliographies. Amara has already found a primary source and a secondary source and needs a tertiary source. She has four other items on her desk, gathered from the school library and an online research database.

Which item is a tertiary source?
o: A medical encyclopedia entry that briefly summarizes what asthma is
A review article that compares the results of several asthma studies
A journal article reporting the results of the authors' own survey of parents
A recorded interview in which a researcher describes her asthma study
w: Encyclopedias are tertiary sources: they compile and condense information from primary and secondary sources into brief reference entries.

n.1: A review article analyzes and summarizes other researchers' studies, which makes it a secondary source.
n.2: An article reporting the authors' own survey is original research, a primary source.
n.3: A researcher describing her own study firsthand is a primary source.

q:
Leah's grandfather was just told he has type 2 diabetes, and she wants reliable information about meal planning to share with him. Her search turns up four websites, listed with what she can tell about each.
Site 1: a .gov page from a national health agency, reviewed by physicians, updated this year
Site 2: a .org page from a group that sells a meal-replacement shake, updated this year
Site 3: a personal blog by a man who manages his diabetes with diet, updated last month
Site 4: a .edu page written by a nutrition student for a class project in 2009

Which site is most likely to be credible?
o: Site 3, because it reflects personal experience with the condition
Site 1, because it is current, reviewed, and from a health authority
Site 4, because .edu sites are written by universities and are reliable
Site 2, because nonprofit .org sites do not sell products to readers
w: Site 1 meets the credibility checks: authority (a national health agency), accuracy (physician review), and currency (updated this year).

n.0: One person's experience is anecdotal and not reviewed by experts.
n.2: This page is a student project from 2009, so it lacks expert authority and is out of date.
n.3: A .org address does not guarantee neutrality; this group sells a product, which is a conflict of interest.

q:
A community health worker is updating a handout on recommended vaccines for adults. She finds two sources that disagree about whether a certain booster is recommended for adults over 65. Source A is a chart from the state health department's website, printed in 2014. Source B is the same department's current online schedule, which notes that its advice was revised last spring after new research was published.

Which source should she rely on, and why?
o: Source B, because online sources are generally more accurate than print
Source B, because it is the current version from the same authority
Source A, because it has been in use longer and has been cited more often
Source A, because a printed chart is more reliable than a web page
w: Both sources come from the same authority, so currency decides. Source B reflects the department's latest advice, revised after new research, which matters for health guidance.

n.0: Source B is better because it is current, not because it is online; many online sources are unreliable.
n.2: Age and frequent citation do not outweigh a newer revision from the same authority.
n.3: Format does not decide accuracy; the 2014 chart is simply out of date.

q:
While researching joint supplements for a health class, Marcus finds a polished website called JointHealthFacts. It features charts, quotations from customers, and a list of benefits of a glucosamine product called FlexWell, with a "Buy Now" button on every page. At the bottom of the home page, in small print, a line reads: "This site is owned and operated by FlexWell Nutrition, Inc." The site was updated two months ago.

What is the strongest reason to question this site's credibility?
o: It includes quotations from customers along with its scientific claims.
It is run by the company that profits from sales of the product it praises.
It was last updated two months ago rather than in the past few weeks.
It includes charts and numbers that may be hard for readers to follow.
w: The site's purpose is to sell FlexWell, and it is owned by the maker. That conflict of interest is the strongest reason to doubt that its information is balanced.

n.0: Customer quotations are weak evidence, but the deeper problem is who owns the site and why.
n.2: An update two months ago is reasonably current; the date is not the main problem.
n.3: Charts can be hard to read, but using data is not itself a reason to distrust a source.

q:
Ethan is researching the 1972 flood that destroyed much of downtown Millbrook. At the county historical society, he finds the following items:
A. A photograph of Main Street taken by a newspaper photographer on the day of the flood
B. An oral history interview, recorded in 2005, with a man who was rescued from his roof in 1972
C. A 2022 newspaper article looking back on the flood's 50th anniversary
D. The Millbrook town council minutes from its emergency meeting in June 1972
E. A local history book, published in 1990, with a chapter analyzing the flood
F. A state encyclopedia entry summarizing major floods in the region

Which items are primary sources? Select all that apply.
o: Item E
Item F
Item C
Item D
Item B
Item A
w: The photograph (A) and the council minutes (D) were created during the event. The oral history (B) is an eyewitness account by a survivor, which makes it primary even though it was recorded decades later.

n.0: A history book analyzing the flood interprets primary sources, so it is secondary.
n.1: An encyclopedia entry compiles summaries from other sources, so it is tertiary.
n.2: An anniversary article looks back on and interprets the flood, so it is secondary.

q:
For a research methods class, Sofia reads an article in a peer-reviewed nursing journal. In it, the authors describe a study they conducted at three hospitals, comparing two methods of preventing pressure injuries in 400 patients. The article explains their methods, presents their data in tables, and discusses what their results mean. Sofia lists the article as a secondary source because it was published in a journal and includes the authors' analysis.

Is Sofia's classification correct?
o: No; it is a primary source because the authors report their own original study.
Yes; it is a secondary source because it appeared in a peer-reviewed journal.
Yes; it is a secondary source because it interprets data using statistics.
No; it is a tertiary source because journals are indexed in library databases.
w: A research article in which the authors present their own study and data is a primary source. Analysis of one's own results does not make it secondary; a review of other people's studies would be.

n.1: Publication in a journal does not decide the type; journals publish both primary studies and secondary reviews.
n.2: Researchers analyzing their own data are still reporting original work, so the article stays primary.
n.3: Being indexed in a database does not make an article tertiary; indexes are tertiary, the articles they list are not.

q:
A school nurse is choosing an online article about managing asthma during exercise to send to the families of students on the track team. She has narrowed her search to one article that seems clear and useful, but the page gives few details about where the information came from. Before she shares it, she wants to know whether the article can be trusted.

Which detail would most increase the article's credibility?
o: It was written by a parent whose two children both have asthma.
It has been shared thousands of times on social media this year.
It includes colorful infographics that explain the steps clearly.
It was written by a lung specialist and cites peer-reviewed studies.
w: A qualified author (authority) and citations to peer-reviewed research (accuracy) are core credibility markers.

n.0: A parent's experience is personal and anecdotal; it lacks medical authority.
n.1: Popularity measures reach, not accuracy; misinformation is often widely shared.
n.2: Clear design helps readability but says nothing about whether the content is correct.

q:
A post on a social media site reads: "New study proves that drinking two cups of green tea a day cuts the risk of heart disease in half! Doctors don't want you to know this." The post has been shared 50,000 times and includes a photo of a teacup but no link. Grace's aunt forwards it to her and asks whether she should start drinking green tea every day.

Which step would best help Grace judge whether the claim is accurate?
o: Count how many people have shared or liked the post.
Search for other posts that make the same green tea claim.
Find the original study that the post claims to describe.
Check how many followers the account that posted it has.
w: Going to the original source shows what the study actually found, how it was done, and whether "proves" and "in half" are accurate.

n.0: The number of shares measures popularity, not accuracy.
n.1: Other posts may simply copy the same claim; repetition is not independent confirmation.
n.3: A large following does not make an account reliable on health research.

q:
For a paper on nursing during the American Civil War, Andre is using two sources.
Source A: the diary kept by a volunteer nurse at a Union hospital in Washington, D.C., from 1862 to 1864
Source B: a 2015 book by a historian who compares the diaries of 30 Civil War nurses and explains what they reveal about hospital conditions
His bibliography must label each source correctly.

Which statement correctly classifies both sources?
o: Source A is secondary, and Source B is primary.
Both are primary, since Source B quotes diaries.
Source A is primary, and Source B is secondary.
Source A is primary, and Source B is tertiary.
w: Step 1: the diary is a firsthand account written at the time, so Source A is primary. Step 2: the historian's book analyzes and interprets those diaries, so Source B is secondary.

n.0: This reverses the categories: the diary is the firsthand record, and the book interprets it.
n.1: Quoting primary sources does not make a book primary; its author interprets others' accounts.
n.3: Source B offers original analysis; tertiary sources such as encyclopedias only compile summaries.

q:
From a heart-health handout: Adults should aim for no more than 2,300 milligrams (mg) of sodium a day, and people with high blood pressure are often advised to stay under 1,500 mg. Most of the sodium people eat comes from packaged and restaurant foods rather than from the salt shaker.
Food (one serving) | Sodium
Canned chicken noodle soup | 890 mg
Turkey sandwich on wheat | 1,050 mg
Frozen cheese pizza (2 slices) | 1,210 mg
Garden salad with dressing | 310 mg
Mr. Alvarez has high blood pressure, and his doctor has told him to follow the lower limit.

Based on the handout and the table, which lunch by itself would put Mr. Alvarez over his daily sodium limit?
o: The soup and the salad
The pizza and the salad
The pizza by itself
The sandwich and the salad
w: Step 1: from the handout, his limit is 1,500 mg. Step 2: from the table, pizza plus salad is 1,210 + 310 = 1,520 mg, which is over 1,500. The other lunches total 1,200, 1,360, and 1,210 mg.

n.0: Soup and salad total 890 + 310 = 1,200 mg, under his 1,500 mg limit.
n.2: The pizza alone is 1,210 mg, under 1,500 mg.
n.3: Sandwich and salad total 1,050 + 310 = 1,360 mg, under 1,500 mg.

q:
A news article reports: "Only 31 percent of adults in Lane County got a flu shot last season." The county health department's online dashboard shows these figures for the same season.
Group | Got a flu shot
Adults 18 to 64 | 31%
Adults 65 and older | 67%
All adults 18 and older | 39%
The dashboard notes that its figures include shots given at clinics, pharmacies, and workplaces in the county.

Which statement best explains why the article's figure differs from the dashboard's figure for all adults?
o: The article's figure matches adults 18 to 64 and leaves out older adults.
The dashboard counts shots given in other counties, which raises its total.
The article rounded the dashboard's figure for all adults down to 31 percent.
The article used data from a different flu season than the dashboard did.
w: The article's 31 percent is exactly the dashboard's figure for adults 18 to 64. Leaving out adults 65 and older, who were vaccinated at 67 percent, gives a lower number than the 39 percent for all adults.

n.1: The dashboard says it counts shots given in the county; nothing suggests it includes other counties.
n.2: Rounding 39 cannot produce 31; the article's number matches a different group.
n.3: The passage says the dashboard shows figures for the same season as the article.

q:
Ridgeline Hospital's emergency department has grown busier. In 2019 it recorded about 41,000 visits; last year it recorded about 52,000. Hospital leaders say they will add eight treatment rooms and hire more nurses by next summer.
Emergency visits by time of arrival, last year
7 a.m. to 3 p.m. | 38%
3 p.m. to 11 p.m. | 45%
11 p.m. to 7 a.m. | 17%

What information does the table provide that the passage does not?
o: Which part of the day brings the largest share of emergency visits
Why most patients chose to come to the emergency department
How many treatment rooms the hospital plans to add next summer
How much the total number of yearly visits has grown since 2019
w: The table breaks last year's visits down by time of arrival, showing that 3 p.m. to 11 p.m. has the largest share (45 percent). The passage gives only yearly totals and plans.

n.1: Neither source gives reasons for visits; the table shows only arrival times.
n.2: The eight new rooms are mentioned in the passage, not the table.
n.3: The growth from about 41,000 to about 52,000 visits comes from the passage.

q:
Podcast transcript, Dr. Lena Kim, sleep researcher: "During puberty, teenagers' internal clocks shift later, so many simply aren't sleepy until 11 p.m. or later. Asking a teenager to wake up at 6 is a bit like asking an adult to wake up at 4."

Newspaper article: A survey of 2,000 high school students in the state found that 70 percent slept less than eight hours on school nights. Students whose first class began at 7:30 a.m. averaged 6.8 hours of sleep.

Which statement is supported by both sources?
o: Teenagers' internal clocks shift later during the years of puberty.
Starting school at 9 a.m. would give teenagers two more hours of sleep.
Early school schedules can leave many teenagers short of sleep.
Seventy percent of high school students sleep less than eight hours.
w: Dr. Kim explains that early waking clashes with teenagers' late sleep timing, and the article's data show short sleep, especially with 7:30 a.m. starts. Both point to early schedules cutting teens' sleep.

n.0: This comes from the podcast only; the article does not discuss internal clocks.
n.1: Neither source measures the effect of a 9 a.m. start; this goes beyond both.
n.3: This comes from the article only; Dr. Kim gives no survey figures.

q:
Timeline: Harbor Street Clinic
1998 | Clinic opens with two exam rooms
2004 | Dental services added
2011 | Clinic moves to a larger building on Pier Avenue
2016 | Evening hours begin
2021 | Telehealth visits begin

From the clinic's anniversary newsletter: The year after the clinic moved, it hired its first full-time Spanish interpreter. Two years after hiring the interpreter, it started a diabetes education class. The class became so popular that a second weekly session was added in the same year that evening hours began.

Based on the timeline and the newsletter, in what year did the diabetes education class start?
w: Step 1: the clinic moved in 2011 (timeline), so the interpreter was hired in 2012. Step 2: the class started two years after the hire, in 2014.

n.0: 2016 is when evening hours began and the second session was added, not when the class started.
n.1: 2013 counts two years from the move (2011) instead of from the interpreter's hiring (2012).
n.2: 2012 is the year the interpreter was hired, one step early.

q:
From Lakeview Hospital's sustainability report: Since switching to reusable surgical gowns, the hospital has cut its gown waste by 1,200 pounds per month. (The report counts a month as four weeks.) The reusable gowns are laundered on site and replaced after about 75 uses.
Chart: Hospital waste by category, after the switch (pounds per week)
Packaging | 900
Food | 1,400
Surgical gowns | 150
Other | 600

Based on the report and the chart, about how many pounds of gown waste did the hospital produce per week before the switch?
o: 300 pounds
450 pounds
1,050 pounds
1,350 pounds
w: Step 1: convert the report's monthly cut to weekly: 1,200 / 4 = 300 pounds per week. Step 2: add it to the chart's weekly figure after the switch: 150 + 300 = 450 pounds per week before.

n.0: 300 pounds is the weekly reduction, not the weekly amount before the switch.
n.2: 1,050 subtracts the weekly figure from the monthly cut (1,200 - 150), mixing units and reversing the direction.
n.3: 1,350 adds the monthly cut to a weekly figure (1,200 + 150) without converting units.

q:
Email from Dana Price: The CPR instructor training starts at 9:00 a.m. on Thursday at the County Health Building on Fifth Street. Please arrive 15 minutes early to sign in and pick up your materials. The building is a 10-minute walk from the Fifth Street bus stop.

Route 12 weekday schedule, arrival times at Fifth Street
7:52 a.m. | 8:22 a.m. | 8:37 a.m. | 8:52 a.m. | 9:07 a.m.

Omar is taking Route 12 to the training. Based on the email and the schedule, which is the latest bus he can take and still arrive in time to sign in?
o: The 8:52 a.m. bus
The 8:37 a.m. bus
The 7:52 a.m. bus
The 8:22 a.m. bus
w: Step 1: arriving 15 minutes before 9:00 means being at the building by 8:45. Step 2: with a 10-minute walk, the bus must reach Fifth Street by 8:35. The latest bus that does is the 8:22.

n.0: The 8:52 bus plus the walk arrives at 9:02, which misses sign-in and is late for the start.
n.1: The 8:37 bus plus a 10-minute walk reaches the building at 8:47, after the 8:45 sign-in time.
n.2: The 7:52 bus works, but the question asks for the latest bus that still gets him there in time.

q:
In January, the Westfield Public Library began lending free home blood pressure monitors. The librarian says the program was designed to reach residents who do not see a doctor regularly. Borrowers may fill out an optional survey when they return a monitor.
Month | Monitor loans
January | 18
February | 31
March | 47
April | 52
Optional survey, January to April: 40 percent of borrowers who responded said they had not had their blood pressure checked in the past year.

Which conclusions are supported by the information above? Select all that apply.
o: Most borrowers had not had their blood pressure checked in the past year.
Some borrowers had gone more than a year without a blood pressure check.
Monitor loans increased every month from January through April.
Monitor loans will keep rising every month for the rest of the year.
Borrowers' blood pressure readings improved after they used the monitors.
The library made a total of 148 monitor loans from January through April.
w: Loans rose each month (18, 31, 47, 52) and total 148. The survey shows that 40 percent of respondents had gone a year without a check, so at least some borrowers had.

n.0: Forty percent of respondents is less than half, so "most" is not supported.
n.3: The data stop in April and growth slowed sharply (up 13, then 16, then only 5), so a rise every month is not supported.
n.4: Neither source reports any blood pressure readings or changes.

q:
From a city magazine article: "Since the city launched its bike-share program in 2022, bike commuting has more than doubled."

U.S. Census survey: share of city workers who commute by bike
2021 | 1.8%
2022 | 2.1%
2023 | 2.6%
2024 | 3.0%

The census figures are estimates for the same city, based on a yearly survey of households; the 2021 figure was collected before the program existed.

Which statement best describes how the census data relate to the article's claim?
o: The data show a rise in bike commuting since 2022, but less than a doubling.
The data confirm that bike commuting more than doubled after the 2022 launch.
The data cannot be compared with the claim because they cover another city.
The data show that bike commuting declined after the program was launched.
w: From 2022 to 2024 the share rose from 2.1 to 3.0 percent, an increase of about 43 percent. That is real growth but well short of doubling (which would be 4.2 percent).

n.1: Doubling 2.1 percent would require 4.2 percent; the data reach 3.0.
n.2: The passage states that the census figures are for the same city.
n.3: The share rose every year after 2022, so the data show growth, not decline.

q:
Report A, from the state health department: 48 percent of adults in the state get regular exercise, defined as at least 150 minutes of moderate activity each week.

Report B, from a fitness company: 72 percent of adults in the state exercise regularly, defined as working out at least once a week for any length of time.

Both reports surveyed randomly selected adults in the same state during the same year, and both asked about exercise over the past month.

Which statement best explains the difference between the two reports' findings?
o: Report B's definition of regular exercise is easier to meet.
Report A counted adults over age 65 and left out younger adults.
The fitness company rounded its figure up to the nearest ten.
Report B surveyed adults in a different year than Report A did.
w: Report A requires 150 minutes a week; Report B counts anyone who works out once a week for any length of time. A looser definition counts more people, which explains the higher percentage.

n.1: Nothing in the passage limits Report A to older adults; it describes adults in the state.
n.2: 72 is not a multiple of ten, so it was not rounded to the nearest ten, and rounding could not explain a 24-point gap.
n.3: The passage says both reports surveyed adults in the same year.

q:
Recipe card: Trail Mix (makes 4 servings)
Combine the entire bag of oat granola with 1 cup of mixed nuts and 1/2 cup of raisins. The nuts and raisins together contain 800 calories.

Nutrition label on the bag of granola
Serving size | 1/4 cup
Servings per container | 8
Calories per serving | 120

Jada makes the recipe exactly as written and divides it into the 4 servings the card describes.

Based on the recipe card and the label, about how many calories are in one serving of Jada's trail mix?
o: 230 calories
1,760 calories
960 calories
440 calories
w: Step 1: the whole bag of granola is 8 servings x 120 = 960 calories. Step 2: add the nuts and raisins: 960 + 800 = 1,760 calories, divided into 4 servings = 440 calories each.

n.0: 230 uses one label serving of granola (120 + 800 = 920, divided by 4) instead of the whole bag.
n.1: 1,760 is the total for the whole recipe, before dividing into 4 servings.
n.2: 960 is the calories in the whole bag of granola, not one serving of trail mix.

q:
Survey of 400 volunteers at Grandview Hospital: "How did you first hear about our volunteer program?"
Friend or family member | 45%
Hospital website | 25%
Social media | 20%
Newspaper ad | 10%

At a planning meeting, the volunteer coordinator said she wants to spend most of next year's outreach budget on newspaper ads. "The newspaper brought in 40 volunteers," she said, "which is more than we expected."

Which statement best combines the survey results with the coordinator's statement?
o: Her figure of 40 conflicts with the survey, which shows only 10.
Her 40 volunteers are accurate but are the smallest group in the survey.
The newspaper brought in more volunteers than social media did.
Most volunteers first heard about the program through online sources.
w: Ten percent of 400 is 40, so her figure matches the survey. But the newspaper is the smallest source; friends and family (180), the website (100), and social media (80) each brought in more volunteers.

n.0: This treats 10 percent as a count; 10 percent of 400 volunteers is 40, matching her figure.
n.2: Social media accounts for 20 percent, or 80 volunteers, twice the newspaper's 40.
n.3: The website and social media together make up 45 percent, which is less than half.

q:
Tanya's four-year-old son, who weighs 36 pounds, has a fever. The pediatrician's nurse told her by phone that she may give him children's acetaminophen, but the office is now closed for the night. Tanya has a new, unopened bottle of the medicine at home and wants to be sure she gives the correct amount for his weight. She considers four sources of information.

Which source should Tanya rely on for the dose?
o: A pediatric medicine handbook from 2009 on her home bookshelf
The dosing chart printed on the label of the new bottle of medicine
A parenting forum where other parents post the doses they give
A magazine article about caring for young children with fevers
w: The label on the product she will actually use is specific to that medicine's strength, current, and approved for use, so it is the authoritative source for the dose.

n.0: A 2009 handbook may not match the strength of today's product; for doses, currency matters.
n.2: Forum posts are anecdotal and may involve different products, strengths, or weights.
n.3: A general magazine article is not specific to this product and is not an authoritative dosing source.

q:
Jamal starts a new job at a medical office next Monday and plans to ride the Route 4 bus. At the start of this month, the city changed the times and stops on several bus routes. He has found four sources: a printed system map his roommate picked up last year, the transit authority's website, a blog where a regular rider reviews city bus routes, and a ride-share app that estimates travel times.

Which source will most reliably give Jamal the Route 4 departure times for next Monday?
o: The printed system map from last year, which lists every bus route
The rider's blog, which describes the usual delays on each route
The transit authority's website, which posts the current schedules
The ride-share app, which estimates door-to-door travel times
w: The transit authority runs the buses and posts the current schedule, which reflects this month's changes. It is both the most authoritative and the most current source.

n.0: Last year's map predates this month's changes, so its times may be wrong.
n.1: A rider's blog is unofficial and may not reflect the new schedule.
n.3: A ride-share app estimates car travel, not bus departure times.

q:
For a history project on nurses in World War I, Paige wants to explain how Lena Harlow, an American army nurse, felt about working near the front lines in France. Her teacher has asked students to present the nurse's own words and feelings rather than someone else's account of them. The school library has several items about Harlow and about nursing in the war.

Which source would best meet Paige's purpose?
o: A collection of the letters Harlow wrote home from France
A textbook chapter on the role of nurses in World War I
A biography of Harlow written in 1985 by her grand-niece
An encyclopedia entry that summarizes Harlow's nursing career
w: Letters Harlow wrote from France are a primary source in her own words, recorded at the time, which is exactly what the assignment asks for.

n.1: A textbook chapter describes nurses in general and is secondary.
n.2: Even a family member's biography is a secondary account that interprets Harlow's experience.
n.3: An encyclopedia entry is a tertiary summary, not Harlow's own words.

q:
While studying for an anatomy quiz, Rosa comes across the word epistaxis in her textbook. The chapter uses the word several times but never shows how to say it. Tomorrow she will present a case study to her study group, and she wants to pronounce the word correctly and confirm whether it is a noun or a verb before she uses it.

Which source would best help Rosa?
o: The index of her textbook
An almanac of health statistics
A thesaurus of medical terms
A medical dictionary
w: A dictionary gives a word's pronunciation, part of speech, and definition, which is exactly what Rosa needs.

n.0: An index lists the pages where a term appears; it does not show pronunciation or part of speech.
n.1: An almanac compiles facts and figures, not word pronunciations.
n.2: A thesaurus lists words with similar meanings; it is not the place to find pronunciation.

q:
Carlos is writing a paper on his state's rules about how many hours a week 16-year-olds may work during the school year. He knows the legislature changed the rules two years ago. He has found a 2015 newspaper article on teen work hours, a blog post by a law firm that advertises its employment services, an encyclopedia article on child labor laws in the United States, and the state labor department's website.

Which source should Carlos use to state the current rule accurately?
o: The law firm's blog post, because lawyers write it for readers with legal questions
The encyclopedia article, because it summarizes child labor laws in every state
The state labor department's website, because it posts the state's current rules
The 2015 newspaper article, because it reports on teen work hours in his state
w: The state agency that enforces the rules publishes them officially, and its website reflects the change made two years ago. It is the most authoritative and current source.

n.0: A law firm's promotional blog may be accurate, but it is not the official source and has a business purpose.
n.1: A general encyclopedia article on national laws is less specific and may not reflect his state's recent change.
n.3: An article from 2015 predates the change two years ago, so it may describe the old rule.

q:
For a public health class, Mei must report how many cases of Lyme disease were reported in her county last year. She has found a national magazine feature on the spread of tick-borne illness, the state health department's online table of reported cases by county and year, a 2006 textbook on infectious diseases, and a widely shared social media post claiming that her county has "the worst tick problem in America."

Which source is best for Mei's purpose?
o: The state health department's table of reported cases by county
The 2006 textbook chapter on infectious diseases and how they spread
The national magazine feature on the spread of tick-borne illness
The widely shared social media post about her county's tick problem
w: Mei needs a specific, recent, local figure. The state health department collects reported cases and publishes them by county and year, so it is specific, current, and authoritative.

n.1: A 2006 textbook cannot report last year's cases.
n.2: A national feature is unlikely to give last year's count for her county and is not the official record.
n.3: A viral post is unsourced and makes a vague, sensational claim rather than giving a count.

q:
Daniela is writing a research paper on how well the shingles vaccine prevents shingles in adults over 50. Her instructor requires sources that are authoritative, current, and free of conflicts of interest, and warns that papers relying on personal stories or advertising will lose points. The paper is due in three weeks and must cite at least two sources on the vaccine's results. Daniela has gathered six possible sources.

Which sources meet her instructor's requirements? Select all that apply.
o: An online forum where adults describe side effects they experienced
A 1995 encyclopedia entry describing shingles and its symptoms
The CDC's current web page on how well the shingles vaccine works
A 2023 peer-reviewed study comparing vaccinated and unvaccinated adults
A magazine interview with an actor who received the vaccine
A television commercial produced by the vaccine's manufacturer
w: A recent peer-reviewed study is authoritative and current, and a federal public health agency's current page is authoritative with no product to sell. Both fit the instructor's criteria.

n.0: Forum posts are personal stories, which the instructor specifically warned against.
n.1: A 1995 entry is not current and cannot address how well today's vaccine works.
n.4: An actor's experience is anecdotal and is not expert evidence.
n.5: An advertisement from the manufacturer has a financial interest in the message.

q:
Andre has just been assigned a group project on sickle cell disease, a topic he knows little about. Before he reads the detailed research articles his group has collected, he wants a short, reliable overview of what the disease is, how it is inherited, and its main symptoms, so that he can follow the technical terms in those articles. His group meets on Thursday to divide up the reading.

Which source would best serve Andre's purpose?
o: A patient's blog about daily life with sickle cell disease
A current medical encyclopedia entry on sickle cell disease
An article reporting a new gene therapy trial in 40 patients
A news story about a fundraising walk for sickle cell research
w: A current encyclopedia entry is a tertiary source designed to give a broad, reliable overview of a topic, which is exactly what Andre needs before reading detailed research.

n.0: A personal blog gives one person's experience, not a reliable overview of the disease.
n.2: A single trial report is primary research on one narrow question and assumes the background Andre lacks.
n.3: A story about a fundraiser does not explain the disease, its inheritance, or symptoms.

q:
Before her baby is born, Hannah wants to choose a rear-facing car seat that performs well in crashes. She has found the websites of three car seat makers, a federal safety agency's page that compares the results of crash tests it ran on many seats, an online store's list of best-selling car seats, and a video by a popular parenting influencer who was paid by one brand to review its seat.

Which source is most reliable for comparing crash safety?
o: The car seat makers' websites, because they know their own products best
The influencer's video, which shows the seat being installed and used
The federal safety agency's page, which compares results of its crash tests
The online store's list of best sellers, which shows what parents choose
w: An independent government agency that runs the same crash tests on many seats provides authoritative, comparable data with no product to sell.

n.0: Each maker has a financial interest in promoting its own seat, and their claims are not directly comparable.
n.1: The influencer was paid by the brand, which is a conflict of interest, and a video demonstration is not crash testing.
n.3: Sales rankings show popularity, not crash performance.

q:
The Okafor family is planning a day hike in the mountains tomorrow and wants to know whether thunderstorms are expected on the trail in the afternoon. They have found a National Weather Service seasonal outlook calling for a wetter-than-normal summer, the National Weather Service forecast for the hiking area that was updated this morning, this morning's forecast for their home city two hours' drive away, and a park ranger's post from yesterday about muddy conditions on the trail.

Which source should the family use?
o: The park ranger's post from yesterday about muddy conditions on the trail
This morning's forecast for their home city, two hours' drive from the trail
The National Weather Service forecast for the hiking area, updated this morning
The National Weather Service seasonal outlook calling for a wetter summer
w: The hiking-area forecast meets every need: it is current (updated this morning), covers the exact place and day, and comes from the national weather authority.

n.0: The ranger's post concerns the trail but describes yesterday's ground conditions, not a forecast of tomorrow's storms.
n.1: This forecast is current but covers a city two hours away; it does not describe afternoon storms in the mountains where they will hike.
n.3: The outlook comes from the right agency, but it covers the whole season, not tomorrow afternoon in the hiking area.

q:
Isabel plans to apply to registered nursing programs in her state for next fall. She needs a complete list of the state's approved programs and each program's current admission requirements, including the minimum TEAS score it expects. Her school counselor has warned her that requirements often change from one year to the next. She has bookmarked several sources to check before the first application deadline.

Which choice would best give Isabel the information she needs?
o: An encyclopedia article explaining the different types of nursing degrees
An online forum where applicants post the TEAS scores that got them admitted
The state board's list of approved programs and each school's admissions page
A national magazine ranking and a college guidebook, both from three years ago
w: Step 1: the state board of nursing is the authority that approves programs, so its list is complete and official. Step 2: each school's own admissions page gives its current requirements for next fall.

n.0: An encyclopedia explains degree types in general; it does not list programs or their requirements.
n.1: Applicants' reported scores are anecdotal and are not the schools' official requirements.
n.3: Both are three years old and requirements change yearly; neither is the official list of approved programs or a school's current requirements.

q:
Marisol, a nursing student, is preparing a teaching sheet for a patient who has just been prescribed a new blood thinner. She wants to list the foods and other medicines that can interact with it. Her options are the official prescribing information published with the drug, a health news website's article about the drug's approval, a popular health app's summary written by its staff, and a pharmacology textbook printed before the drug was approved.

Which source is best for this purpose?
o: The official prescribing information for the drug
The pharmacology textbook printed before approval
The health news article about the drug's approval
The health app's summary written by its staff
w: The official prescribing information lists the drug's known interactions in detail and is the authoritative, product-specific source.

n.1: A textbook printed before the drug was approved cannot include it.
n.2: A news article about approval gives a general story, not a complete list of interactions.
n.3: An app's staff summary is secondhand and may leave out details.
